chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — Venice. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Antonio, Salarino and Solanio.]

ANTONIO. Honestly, I don't know why I'm so sad. It wears me out, and you say it wears you out too. But how I caught it, found it, or came by it—what it's made of, where it was born—that I still have to learn. And this dull-witted sadness makes me such a stranger to myself that I can barely recognize who I am.

SALARINO. Your mind is out on the ocean, where your merchant ships, with their grand sails like noblemen and rich citizens floating along, or like pageant floats on the water, look down on the smaller trading vessels that bow and curtsy to them as they sweep past on their woven wings.

SOLANIO. Believe me, sir, if I had a venture like that out at sea, the better part of my heart would be abroad with my hopes. I'd be constantly plucking grass to test the wind, poring over maps for ports and piers and roads, and every object that might make me fear bad luck for my ships would, without doubt, make me sad.

SALARINO. Just the breath of my own breath cooling my soup would chill me into a fever when I thought what damage a real wind might do at sea. I couldn't watch the sand running through an hourglass without thinking of shallows and sandbanks—seeing my rich ship the Andrew run aground, her tall mast bowed lower than her ribs to kiss her burial. If I went to church and saw that holy stone building, wouldn't I immediately think of dangerous rocks that need only graze my gentle ship's side to scatter all her spices on the current, dress the roaring water in my silks, and—in a word—turn what was just now worth a fortune into nothing? Could I have the thought to imagine all this and not have the thought that, if it actually happened, it would make me sad? Don't tell me otherwise. I know Antonio is sad worrying about his cargo.

ANTONIO. Believe me, I'm not. I thank my luck for it—my ventures aren't trusted to one ship, or one port, and my entire estate doesn't ride on this year's fortunes. So my merchandise isn't what's making me sad.
SALARINO. Then you're in love.
ANTONIO. Oh, please!

SALARINO. Not in love either? Then let's just say you're sad because you're not cheerful—and it would be just as easy for you to laugh and dance and say you're cheerful because you're not sad. Now, by two-faced Janus, nature has framed strange creatures in her time: some who will forever peek through their squinting eyes and laugh like parrots at a bagpiper, and others with such a sour look that they won't crack a smile even if old Nestor swore the joke was hilarious.
[Enter Bassanio, Lorenzo and Gratiano.]
SOLANIO. Here comes Bassanio, your noble kinsman, with Gratiano and Lorenzo. Farewell—we'll leave you now in better company.
SALARINO. I would have stayed until I'd cheered you up, if worthier friends hadn't beaten me to it.
ANTONIO. Your worth means a great deal to me. I take it your own business is calling, and you're using the chance to slip away.
SALARINO. Good morning, my good lords.
BASSANIO. Good sirs, when shall we laugh together? Tell me, when? You're becoming awfully distant. Does it have to be this way?
SALARINO. We'll arrange our free time around yours.
[Exit Salarino and Solanio.]
LORENZO. My Lord Bassanio, now that you've found Antonio, the two of us will leave you. But at dinnertime, please remember where we're supposed to meet.
BASSANIO. I won't let you down.
GRATIANO. You don't look well, Signior Antonio. You take the world too seriously. The people who buy success with too much worry end up losing it. Believe me, you've changed remarkably.
ANTONIO. I treat the world as exactly what it is, Gratiano—a stage where every man must play a part, and mine happens to be a sad one.

GRATIANO. Let me play the fool then. Let old wrinkles come from laughter and merriment, and let my liver be warmed by wine rather than my heart chilled by mortifying groans. Why should a man whose blood runs warm sit like his grandfather carved in alabaster? Sleep through life while wide awake? Get sick from being sour-tempered? I'll tell you what, Antonio—I love you, and it's my love that's speaking—there's a type of man whose face stays smooth and still like a stagnant pond, and who deliberately keeps quiet, hoping to be dressed up in a reputation for wisdom, dignity, and deep thinking, as if to say, "I am Sir Oracle, and when I open my mouth, let no dog bark." Oh Antonio, I know men who are reputed wise only because they say nothing—because I'm very sure that if they did speak, it would almost damn the ears that heard them, and make their listeners call them fools. I'll tell you more about this another time. But don't go fishing for that empty reputation with this melancholy bait. Come on, good Lorenzo. Farewell for now. I'll finish my lecture after dinner.
LORENZO. Well, we'll leave you then until dinnertime. I must be one of these silent wise men, since Gratiano never lets me get a word in.
GRATIANO. Keep me company for two more years and you won't even know the sound of your own voice.
ANTONIO. Farewell. I'll turn into a talker just to keep up.
GRATIANO. Thanks, honestly—because silence is only worthwhile in a dried ox-tongue, or in a girl no one wants to marry.
[Exit Gratiano and Lorenzo.]
ANTONIO. Was there anything in all that?

BASSANIO. Gratiano talks an infinite amount of nothing—more than any other man in Venice. His real points are like two grains of wheat hidden in two bushels of chaff: you can search all day before you find them, and once you do, they're not worth the trouble.
ANTONIO. All right, tell me now—who is this lady you swore a secret pilgrimage to, the one you promised today to tell me about?

BASSANIO. You know already, Antonio, how much I've damaged my estate by keeping up a grander lifestyle than my modest means could sustain. I'm not complaining now about being cut off from such a noble standard of living—my main concern is to get honestly clear of the great debts that my somewhat too-extravagant life has saddled me with. I owe you the most, Antonio, in both money and love, and from your love I take the warrant to unload all my plans and schemes for getting free of the debts I owe.

ANTONIO. Please, good Bassanio, let me hear them. And if your plan, like you yourself, stays within the bounds of honor, then be assured my purse, my person, my furthest resources are all open and available to you.

BASSANIO. In my schooldays, when I lost one arrow, I would shoot a second arrow the same way, watching more carefully, to find the first—and by risking both, I often found both. I bring up this childhood example because what follows is pure honesty. I owe you a great deal, and like a willful young man, what I owe I've lost. But if you would shoot another arrow the same way you shot the first, I have no doubt—since I'll watch the aim—I'll either find both or bring your second risk safely back, and gratefully remain in your debt for the first.

ANTONIO. You know me well, and you're just wasting time wrapping my love up in formalities. Honestly, you wrong me more by questioning my willingness to do everything I can than if you'd squandered everything I own. So just tell me what I should do that you know I'm able to do, and I'm ready to do it. Speak.

BASSANIO. In Belmont there's a lady richly left a fortune—and she is beautiful, and, more than that word can carry, of wonderful virtues. Sometimes from her eyes I received fair, silent messages. Her name is Portia—no less worthy than Cato's daughter, Brutus's Portia. The wide world isn't ignorant of her worth either: the four winds blow in from every coast bringing famous suitors, and her sunny locks hang on her temples like a golden fleece, which makes her home of Belmont the shore of Colchis, and many Jasons come questing for her. Oh, Antonio, if only I had the means to compete on equal footing with one of them, I have a strong feeling I'd be lucky enough to succeed.

ANTONIO. You know that all my fortune is at sea. I don't have ready money or goods to raise an immediate sum. So go out and see what my credit in Venice can do—it will be stretched to the absolute limit to outfit you for Belmont and fair Portia. Go now and inquire, and I will too, to find where money is, and I have no doubt I'll get it on my reputation or as a personal favor.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — Belmont. A room in Portia’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Portia with her waiting-woman Nerissa.]
PORTIA. Honestly, Nerissa, my little body is tired of this great world.

NERISSA. You'd be even more tired, sweet madam, if your miseries were as plentiful as your good fortunes are. And yet, as far as I can see, those who are sick from too much abundance are just as miserable as those who starve with nothing. It's no small happiness, then, to be seated in the middle. Excess brings white hairs sooner, but a modest sufficiency lives longer.
PORTIA. Good points, and well delivered.
NERISSA. They'd be better if well followed.

PORTIA. If doing were as easy as knowing what would be good to do, chapels would be churches and poor men's cottages princes' palaces. It's a good preacher who follows his own instructions. I can more easily teach twenty people what would be good to do than be one of those twenty following my own teaching. The brain may invent laws for the blood, but a hot temper leaps over a cold decree. Madness, the young hare, easily skips over the snares set by good counsel, the cripple. But all this reasoning isn't the way to choose me a husband. Oh me, the word "choose"! I can't choose who I want or refuse who I dislike—the will of a living daughter is constrained by the will of a dead father. Isn't it hard, Nerissa, that I can neither pick one nor refuse any?

NERISSA. Your father was always virtuous, and holy men have good inspirations on their deathbeds. So the lottery he devised in these three chests of gold, silver, and lead—where whoever chooses according to his intention chooses you—will doubtless never be chosen correctly by anyone except the man you'll rightly love. But how warm are your feelings toward any of these princely suitors who have already arrived?
PORTIA. Please go through them one by one, and as you name them, I'll describe them, and from my description you can gauge my feelings.
NERISSA. First, there's the Neapolitan prince.

PORTIA. Ah, that one is a colt indeed—he does nothing but talk about his horse, and he counts it a great point in his favor that he can shoe it himself. I'm rather afraid his mother had a fling with a blacksmith.
NERISSA. Then there's the County Palatine.

PORTIA. He does nothing but frown, as if to say, "If you don't want me, suit yourself." He hears funny stories and doesn't smile. I'm afraid he'll turn into the weeping philosopher when he gets old, being so full of unmannerly sadness already in his youth. I'd rather be married to a skull with a bone in its mouth than to either of those two. God protect me from them both!
NERISSA. What do you say about the French lord, Monsieur Le Bon?

PORTIA. God made him, so let him pass for a man. Honestly, I know it's a sin to be a mocker, but him! Why, he has a better horse than the Neapolitan's, and a worse habit of frowning than the Count Palatine. He's every man and no man at once. If a thrush sings, he immediately starts capering. He'd fence with his own shadow. If I married him, I'd be marrying twenty husbands. If he'd scorn me, I'd forgive him, because even if he loved me to madness, I could never return it.
NERISSA. What about Falconbridge, the young baron of England?

PORTIA. You know I say nothing to him, because he doesn't understand me, and I don't understand him. He has neither Latin, French, nor Italian, and you'd swear in court that my English is worth only a penny. He looks like a proper gentleman in a portrait—but alas, who can hold a conversation with a silent picture? How oddly he's dressed! I think he bought his doublet in Italy, his round hose in France, his hat in Germany, and his manners from everywhere.
NERISSA. What do you think of the Scottish lord, his neighbor?

PORTIA. That he has a neighborly charity in him—he borrowed a box on the ear from the Englishman, and swore he'd pay him back when he was able. I think the Frenchman went his guarantor, and signed on for another.
NERISSA. How do you like the young German, the Duke of Saxony's nephew?

PORTIA. Awful in the morning when he's sober, and most awful in the afternoon when he's drunk. At his best, he's a little worse than a man; at his worst, he's little better than a beast. And whatever the worst that could happen, I hope I can manage to do without him.
NERISSA. If he should offer to choose, and choose the right casket, you'd be refusing to perform your father's will if you refused to accept him.

PORTIA. Therefore, just to be safe, please set a deep glass of Rhenish wine on the wrong casket. Because if there's a devil inside him and that temptation outside, I know he'll choose it. I'll do anything, Nerissa, before I'll marry a sponge.

NERISSA. You needn't fear, lady, having any of these lords. They've informed me of their decisions—which is to return home and trouble you with no more wooing, unless you can be won by some means other than your father's casket condition.

PORTIA. If I live to be as old as the Sibyl, I'll die as chaste as Diana, unless I'm won according to the terms of my father's will. I'm glad this batch of suitors are so reasonable—there's not one among them whose absence I don't adore. And I pray God grant them a smooth departure.
NERISSA. Don't you remember, lady, in your father's time, a Venetian, a scholar and a soldier, who came here in the company of the Marquis of Montferrat?
PORTIA. Yes, yes—it was Bassanio, I think, that was his name.
NERISSA. Exactly, madam. Of all the men my foolish eyes ever looked upon, he was the most deserving of a fair lady.
PORTIA. I remember him well, and I remember him as worthy of your praise.
[Enter a Servingman.]
Well now—what news?

SERVINGMAN. The four strangers are seeking you, madam, to take their leave. And a messenger has come ahead from a fifth, the Prince of Morocco, who brings word that the Prince his master will be here tonight.

PORTIA. If I could welcome the fifth with as good a heart as I can bid the other four farewell, I'd be glad of his arrival. If he has the character of a saint and the complexion of a devil, I'd rather he confessed me than married me. Come, Nerissa. You there, lead the way. As we shut the gate on one suitor, another knocks at the door.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — Venice. A public place
paragraphs: [Enter Bassanio with Shylock the Jew.]
SHYLOCK. Three thousand ducats, well.
BASSANIO. Yes, sir, for three months.
SHYLOCK. For three months, well.
BASSANIO. For which, as I told you, Antonio shall be bound.
SHYLOCK. Antonio shall be the guarantor, well.
BASSANIO. Can you help me? Will you do me the favor? May I hear your answer?
SHYLOCK. Three thousand ducats for three months, and Antonio bound.
BASSANIO. Your answer to that?
SHYLOCK. Antonio is a good man.
BASSANIO. Have you heard any accusation to the contrary?

SHYLOCK. Oh, no, no, no, no. When I say he is a good man, I mean for you to understand that he's financially sufficient. Still, his assets are speculative. He has a merchant ship bound for Tripoli, another for the Indies. I also gather from the Rialto that he has a third one in Mexico, a fourth headed for England, and other ventures scattered abroad. But ships are just boards, sailors just men. There are land-rats and water-rats, water-thieves and land-thieves—I mean pirates—and then there's the peril of waters, winds, and rocks. The man, despite all that, is sufficient. Three thousand ducats. I think I can take his bond.
BASSANIO. You can be assured of it.
SHYLOCK. I will be assured of it. And to be assured, I'll think it over. May I speak with Antonio?
BASSANIO. If it pleases you to dine with us.

SHYLOCK. Yes—to smell pork, to eat from that creature which your prophet, the Nazarene, conjured the devil into. I will buy with you, sell with you, talk with you, walk with you, and so on; but I will not eat with you, drink with you, or pray with you. What news on the Rialto? Who is this coming over here?
[Enter Antonio.]
BASSANIO. This is Signior Antonio.
SHYLOCK.
[Aside.] How like a fawning tax-collector he looks!

I hate him because he is a Christian, but more because, in his stupid simplicity, he lends out money without interest and brings down the rate of interest here in Venice. If I can ever catch him at a disadvantage, I'll feed fat the old grudge I bear him. He hates our sacred nation, and he insults me—right where merchants most gather—about my deals and my well-earned profit, which he calls usury. Cursed be my tribe if I forgive him!
BASSANIO. Shylock, do you hear?

SHYLOCK. I'm calculating my present cash, and by rough memory I can't immediately raise the full sum of three thousand ducats. But no matter—Tubal, a wealthy Hebrew of my tribe, will supply me. But wait! How many months do you need? [To Antonio.] Be well, good sir. Your worship was the last man on our lips.

ANTONIO. Shylock, although I neither lend nor borrow by charging or paying interest, yet to meet the urgent needs of my friend, I'll break that custom. [To Bassanio.] Does he know yet how much you need?
SHYLOCK. Yes, yes, three thousand ducats.
ANTONIO. And for three months.
SHYLOCK. I'd forgotten—three months, you told me so. Well then, your bond. And let me see—but listen, I thought you said you neither lend nor borrow at interest.
ANTONIO. I never do.
SHYLOCK. When Jacob grazed his uncle Laban's sheep—this Jacob, from our holy father Abraham, was, as his wise mother arranged on his behalf, the third in line of inheritance; yes, he was the third.
ANTONIO. And what about him? Did he take interest?

SHYLOCK. No, he didn't take interest—not, as you'd put it, directly. Note what Jacob did. When he and Laban had agreed that all the newborn lambs which were streaked and spotted should go as Jacob's wages, the ewes, being in heat at the end of autumn, were turned to the rams. And when the work of breeding was happening between these woolly creatures, the clever shepherd peeled the bark off certain branches and, in the very act of mating, stuck them up before the lustful ewes—who then, conceiving while looking at them, gave birth at lambing time to multicolored lambs, and those were Jacob's. This was a way to prosper, and he was blessed. And profit is a blessing, if men don't steal it.

ANTONIO. This was a venture, sir, that Jacob worked for—a thing not in his power to bring about, but directed and shaped by the hand of heaven. Was this put in Scripture to justify charging interest? Or is your gold and silver ewes and rams?
SHYLOCK. I can't say; I make it breed just as fast. But mark me, signior.

ANTONIO. Take note of this, Bassanio—the devil can quote Scripture for his own purposes. An evil soul producing holy testimony is like a villain with a smiling face, a fine-looking apple rotten at the core. Oh, what a fine exterior falsehood can have!
SHYLOCK. Three thousand ducats—it's a good round sum. Three months out of twelve. Now let me see the rate.
ANTONIO. Well, Shylock, shall we be in your debt?

SHYLOCK. Signior Antonio, many times and often on the Rialto you have railed at me about my money and my interest-charging. Still I've borne it with a patient shrug, because endurance is the badge of all our tribe. You call me misbeliever, cut-throat dog, and spit on my Jewish gabardine—all for using what is my own. Well then, it now turns out you need my help. Go to, then—you come to me and say, "Shylock, we'd like money." You say that—you who voided your spittle on my beard and kicked me as you'd kick a strange cur from your threshold—money is your request? What should I say to you? Shouldn't I say, "Has a dog money? Is it possible a cur can lend three thousand ducats?" Or should I bow low and, in a slave's tone, with bated breath and whispering humbleness, say this: "Fair sir, you spat on me last Wednesday; you kicked me another day; another time you called me dog. And for these courtesies, I'll lend you all this money"?

ANTONIO. I'm just as likely to call you that again, to spit on you again, to kick you too. If you'll lend this money, don't lend it as to your friends—for when did friendship ever take payment of breeding-interest on barren metal from a friend? Lend it rather to your enemy, who, if he defaults, you can with a clearer face exact the penalty from.

SHYLOCK. Look how you storm at me! I want to be friends with you, and have your love, forget the shames you've stained me with, supply your present needs, and take not a penny of interest on my money—and you won't hear me out. This is kindness I'm offering.
BASSANIO. This would be kindness.

SHYLOCK. This kindness I will show. Come with me to a notary. There, sign me your simple bond; and, as a merry joke, if you don't repay me on such-and-such a day, in such-and-such a place, the sum or sums stated in the contract, let the forfeit be named as an equal pound of your fair flesh, to be cut off and taken from whatever part of your body pleases me.
ANTONIO. Agreed, honestly—I'll sign such a bond, and say there's much kindness in the Jew.
BASSANIO. You will not sign such a bond for me. I'd rather stay in my poverty.
ANTONIO. Don't be afraid, man—I won't have to forfeit. Within two months—that's a month before this bond expires—I expect a return of three times three the value of this bond.

SHYLOCK. Oh father Abraham, what these Christians are! Their own harsh dealings teach them to suspect the thoughts of others. Tell me this, please: if he should miss his day, what would I gain by collecting the forfeit? A pound of man's flesh, taken from a man, isn't as valuable, or as profitable, as the flesh of muttons, beefs, or goats. I tell you, to buy his goodwill, I extend this friendship. If he'll take it, so. If not, goodbye—and for my love, please don't wrong me.
ANTONIO. Yes, Shylock, I will sign this bond.

SHYLOCK. Then meet me right away at the notary's. Give him directions for this merry bond, and I'll go and bag the ducats straight away. I need to check on my house, which is left in the unreliable guard of a wasteful servant—and I'll be with you presently.
ANTONIO. Hurry, gentle Jew.
[Exit Shylock.]
This Hebrew will turn Christian—he's growing kind.
BASSANIO. I don't like fair terms with a villain's mind behind them.
ANTONIO. Come on. There can be no cause for alarm in this. My ships come home a month before the deadline.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — Belmont. A room in Portia’s house
paragraphs: [Flourish of cornets. Enter the Prince of Morocco, a tawny Moor all in white, and three or four followers accordingly, with Portia, Nerissa and their train.]

PRINCE OF MOROCCO. Don't dislike me for my complexion—the shaded livery of the burnished sun, to whom I am a neighbor and closely related. Bring me the fairest creature born in the north, where Phoebus's fire scarcely thaws the icicles, and let us make a cut for your love to prove whose blood is reddest, his or mine. I tell you, lady, this face of mine has frightened the brave; by my love I swear the most respected virgins of our country have loved it too. I would not change this color, except to win your favor, my gentle queen.

PORTIA. In matters of choice I'm not guided solely by the dainty direction of a maiden's eyes. Besides, the lottery of my destiny bars me from the right of choosing voluntarily. But if my father hadn't restricted me and bound me by his wit to give myself in marriage to whoever wins me by the means I described, you yourself, renowned Prince, would stand as good a chance with my affection as any suitor I've looked on yet.

PRINCE OF MOROCCO. For even that, I thank you. So please lead me to the caskets to try my fortune. By this scimitar that slew the Sophy and a Persian prince, and that won three battles from Sultan Solyman, I would outstare the sternest eyes that look, outbrave the most daring heart on earth, pluck the young suckling cubs from the she-bear—yes, even mock the lion when he roars for prey—to win you, lady. But alas! If Hercules and his servant Lichas were to play at dice for who was the better man, the higher throw might fall by chance from the weaker hand. So Hercules can be beaten by his attendant, and so may I, with blind Fortune leading me, miss what an unworthier man may obtain, and die of grief.

PORTIA. You must take your chance, and either not attempt to choose at all, or swear before you choose that, if you choose wrong, you'll never speak to any lady afterward about marriage. So consider carefully.
PRINCE OF MOROCCO. I will. Come, bring me to my chance.
PORTIA. First, on to the temple. After dinner your gamble shall be made.
PRINCE OF MOROCCO. Good fortune then, to make me the most blessed or most cursed among men!
[Cornets. Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — Venice. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Launcelet Gobbo, the clown, alone.]

LAUNCELET. Certainly my conscience will allow me to run away from this Jew my master. The fiend is at my elbow tempting me, saying "Gobbo, Launcelet Gobbo, good Launcelet," or "good Gobbo," or "good Launcelet Gobbo, use your legs, take off, run away." My conscience says, "No—be careful, honest Launcelet, be careful, honest Gobbo," or as I said, "honest Launcelet Gobbo, don't run, refuse to run." Well, the very courageous fiend tells me to pack up. "Off with you!" says the fiend. "Away!" says the fiend. "For heaven's sake, rouse up a brave mind," says the fiend, "and run." Well, my conscience, hanging about the neck of my heart, says very wisely, "My honest friend Launcelet, being an honest man's son"—or rather an honest woman's son, since indeed my father had a bit of a taste for it, something on the side, a kind of flavor—well, my conscience says, "Launcelet, don't budge." "Budge," says the fiend. "Don't budge," says my conscience. "Conscience," I say, "you advise well." "Fiend," I say, "you advise well." To be ruled by my conscience, I should stay with the Jew my master, who (God save the mark) is a kind of devil. And to run away from the Jew, I should be ruled by the fiend, who (saving your reverence) is the devil himself. Certainly the Jew is the very devil incarnate, and, in my conscience, my conscience is just a hard kind of conscience to offer to counsel me to stay with the Jew. The fiend gives the friendlier counsel. I will run, fiend; my heels are at your command, I will run.
[Enter Old Gobbo with a basket.]
GOBBO. Master young man, you—please, which is the way to Master Jew's?
LAUNCELET.
[Aside.] Oh heavens, this is my true-begotten father, who, being more
than half-blind, dim-sighted as gravel, doesn't recognize me. I'll have some fun with him.
GOBBO. Master young gentleman, please, which is the way to Master Jew's?
LAUNCELET. Turn right at the next corner, but at the very next turn after that, go left. Marry, at the very next turn, don't turn at all, but go indirectly down to the Jew's house.
GOBBO. By God's saints, that'll be a hard road to find. Can you tell me whether one Launcelet, who lives with him, lives with him or not?
LAUNCELET. Are you talking about young Master Launcelet? [Aside.] Watch this now—now I'll stir up the waters. Are you talking about young Master Launcelet?
GOBBO. Not master, sir, but a poor man's son. His father, though I say it, is an honest, exceedingly poor man, and, God be thanked, comfortable enough.
LAUNCELET. Well, let his father be whatever he is—we're talking about young Master Launcelet.
GOBBO. Your worship's friend, and just plain Launcelet, sir.
LAUNCELET. But please, ergo, old man, ergo, I beseech you—are you talking about young Master Launcelet?
GOBBO. About Launcelet, if it please your mastership.

LAUNCELET. Ergo, Master Launcelet. Don't talk about Master Launcelet, father—because the young gentleman, according to the Fates and Destinies and such curious expressions, the Three Sisters and such branches of learning, is indeed deceased, or, in plain terms, gone to heaven.
GOBBO. Marry, God forbid! The boy was the very staff of my old age, my very prop.
LAUNCELET.
[Aside.] Do I look like a cudgel or a tent-pole, a staff or a prop?
Do you know me, father?
GOBBO. Alas the day! I don't know you, young gentleman, but please tell me—is my boy, God rest his soul, alive or dead?
LAUNCELET. Don't you know me, father?
GOBBO. Alas, sir, I am dim-sighted. I don't know you.

LAUNCELET. No—indeed, even if you had your full eyesight you might fail to recognize me. It's a wise father who knows his own child. Well, old man, I'll tell you news of your son. Give me your blessing. Truth will come to light, murder can't be hidden long, a man's son may be, but in the end the truth will out.
GOBBO. Please, sir, stand up. I'm sure you're not Launcelet, my boy.
LAUNCELET. Please, let's have no more fooling about it—just give me your blessing. I am Launcelet, your boy that was, your son that is, your child that shall be.
GOBBO. I can't believe you are my son.
LAUNCELET. I don't know what to think of that, but I am Launcelet, the Jew's servant, and I'm sure Margery your wife is my mother.

GOBBO. Her name is Margery, indeed. I'll swear, if you're Launcelet, you're my own flesh and blood. Lord be worshipped, what a beard you've got! You have more hair on your chin than Dobbin my cart-horse has on his tail.
LAUNCELET. It would seem then that Dobbin's tail is growing backward. I'm sure he had more hair on his tail than I have on my face the last time I saw him.
GOBBO. Lord, how you're changed! How do you and your master get along? I've brought him a present. How do you get along now?

LAUNCELET. Well, well. But for my own part, since I've made up my mind to run away, I won't rest till I've put some ground behind me. My master is a thoroughgoing Jew. Give him a present! Give him a noose. I'm starving in his service. You can count every finger I have through my ribs. Father, I'm glad you've come—give your present to a certain Master Bassanio, who indeed gives splendid new uniforms. If I don't serve him, I'll run as far as God has any ground. Oh rare fortune, here comes the man! Approach him, father; for I'm a Jew if I serve the Jew any longer.
[Enter Bassanio with Leonardo and a follower or two.]
BASSANIO. You may do so, but make it quick—supper should be ready by five o'clock at the latest. See these letters delivered, get the liveries made, and ask Gratiano to come to my lodging soon.
[Exit a Servant.]
LAUNCELET. Approach him, father.
GOBBO. God bless your worship!
BASSANIO. Many thanks. Do you want something from me?
GOBBO. Here's my son, sir, a poor boy.
LAUNCELET. Not a poor boy, sir, but the rich Jew's servant, who would like, sir—as my father shall specify—
GOBBO. He has a great infection, sir, as one might say, to serve—
LAUNCELET. Indeed, the short and long of it is, I serve the Jew, and have a desire, as my father shall specify—
GOBBO. His master and he (saving your worship's reverence) are scarcely close cousins.
LAUNCELET. To be brief, the very truth is that the Jew, having done me wrong, has caused me—as my father, being I hope an old man, shall "frutify" unto you—
GOBBO. I have here a dish of doves that I'd like to bestow upon your worship, and my request is—
LAUNCELET. In very brief, the request concerns me, as your worship will learn from this honest old man, and though I say so myself—though old man, yet poor man—my father.
BASSANIO. One of you speak for both. What do you want?
LAUNCELET. To serve you, sir.
GOBBO. That is the very defect of the matter, sir.

BASSANIO. I know you well; you've gotten your request. Your master Shylock spoke with me today, and has recommended you—if it's a promotion to leave a rich Jew's service to become the follower of so poor a gentleman.
LAUNCELET. The old proverb is very well divided between my master Shylock and you, sir: you have "the grace of God," sir, and he has "enough."
BASSANIO. You put it well. Go, father, with your son. Take leave of your old master, and find out where my lodging is. [To a Servant.] Give him a livery more decorated than his fellows'—see to it.

LAUNCELET. Father, come inside. I can't get a position, no! I've got no tongue in my head! [Looking at his palm.] Well, if any man in Italy has a finer palm to swear upon a book with, I shall have good fortune. Go to, here's a clear line of life. Here's a small trifle of wives—alas, fifteen wives is nothing; eleven widows and nine maids is a simple income for one man. And then to escape drowning three times, and to be in danger of my life on the edge of a feather-bed—here are simple escapes. Well, if Fortune is a woman, she's a good girl for all this. Father, come—I'll take my leave of the Jew in a twinkling.
[Exit Launcelet and Old Gobbo.]
BASSANIO. Please, good Leonardo, see to this. Once these things are bought and properly stored, return in a hurry, because tonight I'm hosting my most esteemed acquaintance. Hurry, go.
LEONARDO. My best efforts shall be applied to it.
[Enter Gratiano.]
GRATIANO. Where's your master?
LEONARDO. Over there, sir, he's walking.
[Exit.]
GRATIANO. Signior Bassanio!
BASSANIO. Gratiano!
GRATIANO. I have a request to make of you.
BASSANIO. You've got it.
GRATIANO. You mustn't refuse me—I must go with you to Belmont.

BASSANIO. Why then, you must. But listen, Gratiano—you're too wild, too rude, and too loud of voice. Those qualities suit you well enough, and in eyes like ours they don't appear as faults, but where you aren't known, they come across as too unrestrained. Please take pains to soften your bouncy spirit with some cool drops of modesty, in case your wild behavior makes me misunderstood in the place I'm going to, and I lose my hopes.

GRATIANO. Signior Bassanio, listen to me. If I don't adopt a sober manner, talk with respect, and swear only now and then, wear prayer-books in my pocket, look demure—nay, more, while grace is being said cover my eyes thus with my hat, and sigh, and say "amen"; observe all the rules of civility like one well practiced in a solemn demeanor to please his grandmother—never trust me again.
BASSANIO. Well, we shall see how you behave.
GRATIANO. No, but I draw the line at tonight. You shan't judge me by what we do tonight.
BASSANIO. No, that would be a pity. Rather I'd ask you to put on your boldest suit of mirth, because we have friends who intend to be merry. But farewell—I have some business.
GRATIANO. And I must go to Lorenzo and the rest, but we'll visit you at supper time.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — The same. A room in Shylock’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Jessica and Launcelet.]

JESSICA. I'm sorry you'll leave my father like this. Our house is hell, and you, a merry devil, robbed it of some of its tediousness. But fare you well—here's a ducat for you. And, Launcelet, at supper soon you'll see Lorenzo, who is your new master's guest. Give him this letter—do it secretly. And so farewell. I wouldn't want my father to see me talking with you.

LAUNCELET. Goodbye! Tears speak for my tongue, most beautiful pagan, most sweet Jew! If some Christian doesn't play the knave and win you, I'm very much mistaken. But goodbye! These foolish drops are somewhat drowning my manly spirit. Goodbye!
JESSICA. Farewell, good Launcelet.
[Exit Launcelet.]

Alas, what a heinous sin it is in me to be ashamed to be my father's child! But though I'm a daughter to his blood, I'm not to his manners. Oh Lorenzo, if you keep your promise, I'll end this struggle—become a Christian and your loving wife.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — The same. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Gratiano, Lorenzo, Salarino and Solanio.]
LORENZO. No, we'll slip away during supper, get into disguise at my lodging, and be back within an hour.
GRATIANO. We haven't prepared properly.
SALARINO. We haven't arranged for torch-bearers yet.
SOLANIO. It's a poor idea unless it can be cleverly organized, and better in my opinion not attempted at all.
LORENZO. It's only four o'clock now—we have two hours to get ready.
[Enter Launcelet with a letter.]
Friend Launcelet, what's the news?
LAUNCELET. If you'll please to open this, it shall seem to indicate.
LORENZO. I know the handwriting; honestly it's a fair hand, and whiter than the paper it was written on is the fair hand that wrote it.
GRATIANO. Love news, honestly.
LAUNCELET. By your leave, sir.
LORENZO. Where are you going?
LAUNCELET. Marry, sir, to invite my old master the Jew to sup tonight with my new master the Christian.
LORENZO. Wait, take this. Tell gentle Jessica I won't fail her—say it privately. Go, gentlemen.
[Exit Launcelet.]
Will you prepare yourselves for this masque tonight? I'm fixed up with a torch-bearer.
SALARINO. Yes, marry, I'll go take care of it right now.
SOLANIO. And so will I.
LORENZO. Meet me and Gratiano at Gratiano's lodging in about an hour.
SALARINO. Good plan.
[Exit Salarino and Solanio.]
GRATIANO. Wasn't that letter from fair Jessica?

LORENZO. I must tell you all. She's instructed me how to take her from her father's house, what gold and jewels she has gathered, and what page's suit she has ready. If the Jew her father ever comes to heaven, it will be for his gentle daughter's sake. And may misfortune never dare cross her path, unless it does so under this excuse: that she's the child of a faithless Jew. Come, go with me—read this as you walk. Fair Jessica shall be my torch-bearer.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 5 — The same. Before Shylock’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Shylock the Jew and Launcelet his man that was the clown.]

SHYLOCK. Well, you'll see—your own eyes shall be your judge—the difference between old Shylock and Bassanio. What, Jessica!—You won't be allowed to gorge yourself as you've done with me—what, Jessica!—and sleep, and snore, and wear out clothes. Why, Jessica, I say!
LAUNCELET. Why, Jessica!
SHYLOCK. Who tells you to call her? I didn't tell you to call.
LAUNCELET. Your worship used to tell me I could do nothing without being told.
[Enter Jessica.]
JESSICA. Did you call? What do you want?

SHYLOCK. I've been invited out to supper, Jessica. Here are my keys. But why should I go? I'm not invited out of love—they flatter me. But still, I'll go in hatred, to feed off the prodigal Christian. Jessica, my girl, look after my house. I'm very reluctant to go. Something bad is brewing against my peace, because I dreamed of money-bags tonight.
LAUNCELET. I beg you, sir, go. My young master is expecting your reproach.
SHYLOCK. And so do I expect his.

LAUNCELET. And they've conspired together. I won't say you'll see a masque, but if you do, then it wasn't for nothing that my nose started bleeding last Black Monday at six o'clock in the morning—falling that year four years after Ash Wednesday, in the afternoon.

SHYLOCK. What, are there masques? Listen to me, Jessica—lock up my doors, and when you hear the drum and the vile squealing of the crook-necked fife, don't go climbing up to the windows or thrust your head into the public street to gawk at Christian fools with painted faces. Stop my house's ears—I mean my windows. Don't let the sound of shallow foppery enter my sober house. By Jacob's staff I swear I have no inclination for feasting out tonight. But I will go. You go ahead, sirrah. Say I'll come.
LAUNCELET. I'll go ahead, sir. Mistress, look out the window in spite of all this. There will come a Christian by worth a Jewess's eye.
[Exit Launcelet.]
SHYLOCK. What does that fool of Hagar's offspring say, eh?
JESSICA. His words were "Farewell, mistress," nothing else.

SHYLOCK. The clown is kind enough, but a huge eater, snail-slow in profit, and he sleeps by day more than a wildcat. Drones don't hive with me—so I part with him, and part with him to a man I want him to help waste his borrowed purse. Well, Jessica, go inside. Perhaps I'll return right away. Do as I tell you—shut the doors after you. "Fast bind, fast find." A proverb never stale in a thrifty mind.
[Exit.]
JESSICA. Farewell. And if my luck isn't crossed, I have a father, and you have a daughter, lost.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 6 — The same
paragraphs: [Enter the masquers, Gratiano and Salarino.]
GRATIANO. This is the overhang under which Lorenzo asked us to wait.
SALARINO. His appointed hour is almost past.
GRATIANO. And it's a wonder he's late, since lovers always run ahead of the clock.
SALARINO. Oh, Venus's doves fly ten times faster to seal love's new-made bonds than they do to keep faith already pledged!

GRATIANO. That's always true. Who rises from a feast with the same keen appetite they sat down with? Where's the horse that retraces his tedious paces with the same undiminished fire as when he first paced them? All things, in this world, are chased with more spirit than enjoyed. How like a younger son or a prodigal does the be-flagged ship put out from her home harbor, hugged and embraced by the wanton wind! How like the prodigal does she return, with weather-beaten ribs and ragged sails, lean, torn, and beggared by that same wanton wind!
[Enter Lorenzo.]
SALARINO. Here comes Lorenzo—more of this later.

LORENZO. Sweet friends, forgive my long delay. Not I but my affairs have kept you waiting. When you yourselves decide to play the thieves to steal wives, I'll wait just as long for you then. Come closer. Here lives my father-Jew. Ho! Who's inside?
[Enter Jessica above, in boy's clothes.]
JESSICA. Who are you? Tell me, to be certain, though I'll swear I know your voice.
LORENZO. Lorenzo, and your love.
JESSICA. Lorenzo for sure, and my love indeed—for who do I love so much? And now who knows but you, Lorenzo, whether I am yours?
LORENZO. Heaven and your own thoughts are witness that you are.

JESSICA. Here, catch this casket—it's worth the trouble. I'm glad it's night, so you can't look on me, because I'm much ashamed of my transformation. But love is blind, and lovers can't see the pretty follies that they commit—for if they could, Cupid himself would blush to see me transformed like this into a boy.
LORENZO. Come down, because you have to be my torch-bearer.
JESSICA. What! Must I hold a candle to my own shame? They are, in truth, light enough already. Why, this is an office of exposure, love, and I should be hidden.
LORENZO. So you are, sweet, even in the lovely costume of a boy. But come at once, because the secretive night is hurrying away, and we're being expected at Bassanio's feast.
JESSICA. I'll lock up the doors, gild myself with a few more ducats, and be with you straight away.
[Exit above.]
GRATIANO. Now, by my hood, a gentile, and no Jew at all.

LORENZO. Curse me if I don't love her heartily, because she's wise, as far as I can judge her, and beautiful she is, if my eyes tell true, and faithful she is, as she's just proved herself. And therefore, like herself, wise, beautiful, and faithful, she shall be placed in my constant soul.
[Enter Jessica.]
Have you come? On, gentlemen, away! Our masquing companions will be waiting for us by now.
[Exit with Jessica and Salarino.]
[Enter Antonio.]
ANTONIO. Who's there?
GRATIANO. Signior Antonio!

ANTONIO. Oh come, Gratiano! Where are all the rest? It's nine o'clock, our friends are all waiting for you. No masque tonight—the wind has come about; Bassanio is going aboard right away. I've sent twenty men out to look for you.
GRATIANO. I'm glad to hear it. I desire no greater delight than to be under sail and gone tonight.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 7 — Belmont. A room in Portia’s house
paragraphs: [Flourish of cornets. Enter Portia with the Prince of Morocco and both their trains.]
PORTIA. Go, draw aside the curtains and reveal the various caskets to this noble prince. Now make your choice.

PRINCE OF MOROCCO. The first, of gold, which bears this inscription: "Who chooses me shall gain what many men desire." The second, silver, which carries this promise: "Who chooses me shall get as much as he deserves." The third, dull lead, with a warning just as blunt: "Who chooses me must give and hazard all he has." How shall I know if I choose the right one?
PORTIA. One of them contains my picture, prince. If you choose that one, then I am yours along with it.

PRINCE OF MOROCCO. Some god direct my judgment! Let me see. I'll go over the inscriptions again. What does this leaden casket say? "Who chooses me must give and hazard all he has." Must give—for what? For lead? Hazard everything for lead! This casket threatens. Men who risk everything do so in hope of fair gains. A golden mind doesn't stoop to displays of trash. So I won't give or hazard anything for lead. What does the silver say with her virgin hue? "Who chooses me shall get as much as he deserves." As much as he deserves! Pause there, Morocco, and weigh your own value with an even hand. If you are rated according to your reputation, you do deserve enough—and yet enough may not stretch as far as this lady. And yet to be afraid of my own deserving would be a weak undermining of myself. As much as I deserve! Why, that is the lady: I deserve her in birth, in fortune, in graces, and in qualities of breeding. But more than these, in love I deserve her. What if I went no further, but chose right here? Let's see once more this saying engraved in gold: "Who chooses me shall gain what many men desire." Why, that's the lady—all the world desires her. From the four corners of the earth they come to kiss this shrine, this mortal breathing saint. The deserts of Hyrcania and the vast wilds of wide Arabia are now highways for princes to come and view fair Portia. The watery kingdom, whose ambitious crest spits in the face of heaven, is no barrier to stop foreign spirits—they come as if crossing a brook to see fair Portia. One of these three contains her heavenly picture. Is it likely that lead contains her? It would be damnation to think such a base thought. It would be too crude to wrap her shroud in the obscure grave. Or shall I think she's walled up in silver, being ten times less valuable than tried gold? Oh sinful thought! Never was such a rich gem set in anything worse than gold. They have in England a coin called an angel stamped in gold—but that's only engraved on the surface. Here, though, an angel in a golden bed lies wholly within. Give me the key. Here I choose, and may I thrive as I may.
PORTIA. There, take it, prince. And if my likeness lies there, then I am yours.
[He unlocks the golden casket.]
PRINCE OF MOROCCO. Oh hell! What have we here? A skull, within whose empty eye-socket there's a written scroll. I'll read the writing.

All that glitters is not gold, / Often have you heard that told. / Many a man his life has sold / But my outside to behold. / Gilded tombs do worms enfold. / Had you been as wise as bold, / Young in limbs, in judgment old, / Your answer had not been on this scroll. / Fare you well, your suit is cold.
Cold indeed, and labor lost. Then farewell heat, and welcome frost. Portia, adieu! I have too grieved a heart to take a tedious leave. Thus losers depart.
[Exit with his train. Flourish of cornets.]
PORTIA. A gentle riddance. Draw the curtains, go. Let all of his complexion choose me so.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 8 — Venice. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Salarino and Solanio.]
SALARINO. Why, man, I saw Bassanio under sail. With him went Gratiano. And in their ship I'm sure Lorenzo is not.
SOLANIO. The villain Jew with his outcries roused the Duke, who went with him to search Bassanio's ship.

SALARINO. He came too late—the ship was already under sail. But there the Duke was informed that in a gondola were seen together Lorenzo and his amorous Jessica. Besides, Antonio assured the Duke they were not with Bassanio on his ship.

SOLANIO. I never heard a passion so confused, so strange, outrageous, and so variable as the dog Jew uttered in the streets. "My daughter! Oh my ducats! Oh my daughter! Fled with a Christian! Oh my Christian ducats! Justice! The law! My ducats and my daughter! A sealed bag, two sealed bags of ducats, of double ducats, stolen from me by my daughter! And jewels—two stones, two rich and precious stones, stolen by my daughter! Justice! Find the girl, she has the stones on her and the ducats."
SALARINO. Why, all the boys in Venice follow him, crying about his stones, his daughter, and his ducats.
SOLANIO. Good Antonio had better make sure he keeps his deadline, or he'll pay for this.

SALARINO. Marry, well remembered. I was talking with a Frenchman yesterday, who told me that in the narrow seas that part the French and English, there was lost a vessel of our country richly loaded. I thought of Antonio when he told me, and silently wished it wasn't his.
SOLANIO. You'd best tell Antonio what you've heard—but don't do it suddenly, since it may grieve him.

SALARINO. A kinder gentleman doesn't walk the earth. I saw Bassanio and Antonio parting. Bassanio told him he would hurry his return. He answered, "Don't do that. Don't botch your business for my sake, Bassanio—stay the full ripening of the time. And about the Jew's bond he holds on me, don't let it enter your loving mind. Be merry, and employ your chief thoughts in courtship and such fair displays of love as will properly become you there." And even there, his eye welling with tears, he turned his face, put his hand behind him, and with wonderfully tender affection he wrung Bassanio's hand—and so they parted.
SOLANIO. I think he only loves the world for Bassanio's sake. Please, let's go and find him out and lighten his embraced heaviness with some delight or other.
SALARINO. Let's do it.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 9 — Belmont. A room in Portia’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Nerissa and a Servitor.]
NERISSA. Quick, quick, please, draw the curtain straight away. The Prince of Aragon has taken his oath, and is coming to make his choice immediately.
[Flourish of cornets. Enter the Prince of Aragon, his train, and Portia.]

PORTIA. Behold, there stand the caskets, noble Prince. If you choose the one in which I'm contained, our wedding rites shall be solemnized immediately. But if you fail, without further discussion, my lord, you must be gone from here right away.

ARRAGON. I am bound by oath to observe three things: First, never to reveal to anyone which casket I chose; next, if I fail to pick the right casket, never in my life to woo a maid in marriage; lastly, if I fail in my chosen fortune, to leave you immediately and be gone.
PORTIA. To these conditions everyone who comes to gamble for my worthless self has to swear.

ARRAGON. And so have I prepared myself. Fortune now—to my heart's hope! Gold, silver, and base lead. "Who chooses me must give and hazard all he has." You shall look fairer before I give or hazard. What does the golden chest say? Ha! Let me see: "Who chooses me shall gain what many men desire." What many men desire! That "many" may mean the foolish multitude, who choose by appearances, learning no more than the fond eye teaches—who don't see into the interior, but like the swift build in the weather on the outer wall, in the very path of misfortune. I won't choose what many men desire, because I won't fall in with common spirits and rank myself with the barbarous multitudes. Why then, to you, silver treasure-house—tell me once more what title you bear. "Who chooses me shall get as much as he deserves." And well said too. For who would attempt to cheat fortune, and be honorable without the stamp of merit? Let no one presume to wear an undeserved dignity. Oh, if only positions, ranks, and offices weren't derived corruptly, and clear honor were purchased by the merit of the wearer! How many then would have to cover their heads who now stand bareheaded? How many would be commanded who now command? How much low peasantry would then be gleaned from the true seed of honor? And how much honor picked from the chaff and ruin of the times, to be newly polished? Well, but to my choice. "Who chooses me shall get as much as he deserves." I will assume desert. Give me a key for this one, and instantly unlock my fortunes here.
[He opens the silver casket.]
PORTIA. Too long a pause for what you find there.

ARRAGON. What's here? The portrait of a blinking idiot presenting me a scroll! I'll read it. How unlike are you to Portia! How unlike my hopes and my deservings! "Who chooses me shall have as much as he deserves." Did I deserve no more than a fool's head? Is that my prize? Are my merits no better?
PORTIA. To offend and to judge are distinct offices, and of opposite natures.
ARRAGON. What's here?

The fire seven times tried this; / Seven times tried that judgment is / That did never choose amiss. / Some there be that shadows kiss; / Such have but a shadow's bliss. / There be fools alive, I know, / Silvered o'er, and so was this. / Take whatever wife you will to bed, / I will ever be your head. / So be gone; you are dispatched.
I shall appear even more a fool the longer I linger here. With one fool's head I came to woo, but I go away with two. Sweet, adieu! I'll keep my oath, and patiently bear my anger.
[Exit Arragon with his train.]
PORTIA. Thus has the candle singed the moth. Oh, these deliberate fools! When they do choose, they have just enough wit to lose.
NERISSA. The ancient saying is no heresy: hanging and wiving go by destiny.
PORTIA. Come, draw the curtain, Nerissa.
[Enter a Messenger.]
MESSENGER. Where is my lady?
PORTIA. Here. What does my lord want?

MESSENGER. Madam, there has arrived at your gate a young Venetian, one who comes ahead to announce the approaching arrival of his lord, from whom he brings substantial greetings—that is, besides compliments and courteous words, gifts of rich value. Yet I've never seen so promising an ambassador of love. A day in April never came so sweet, to signal how lavish summer was at hand, as this advance-runner comes before his lord.

PORTIA. No more, please. I'm half afraid you'll say in a moment he's some kin to you, you spend such holiday wit in praising him. Come, come, Nerissa—because I long to see quick Cupid's messenger who comes so mannerly.
NERISSA. Bassanio, Lord of Love, if it be your will!
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Venice. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Solanio and Salarino.]
SOLANIO. Now, what news on the Rialto?

SALARINO. Why, it still circulates there unchallenged that Antonio has had a richly loaded ship wrecked in the narrow seas—the Goodwins, I think they call the place, a very dangerous shoal and fatal, where, they say, the carcasses of many a tall ship lie buried—if my gossip Rumor is an honest woman of her word.

SOLANIO. I wish she were as lying a gossip about that as one who ever cracked ginger, or made her neighbors believe she wept for the death of a third husband. But it's true, without any excess of words or going off the plain highway of plain talk, that the good Antonio, the honest Antonio—oh, that I had a title good enough to keep his name company!—
SALARINO. Come, the full stop.
SOLANIO. Ha, what's that you say? Why, the upshot is, he has lost a ship.
SALARINO. I hope that's the end of his losses.
SOLANIO. Let me say "amen" right now, before the devil crosses my prayer—because here he comes in the likeness of a Jew.
[Enter Shylock.]
How now, Shylock, what news among the merchants?
SHYLOCK. You knew, none so well, none so well as you, of my daughter's flight.
SALARINO. That's true—I, for my part, knew the tailor who made the wings she flew with.
SOLANIO. And Shylock, for his own part, knew the bird was fledged—and then it's the nature of them all to leave the nest.
SHYLOCK. She is damned for it.
SALARINO. That's certain, if the devil may be her judge.
SHYLOCK. My own flesh and blood to rebel!
SOLANIO. Out on it, old carrion! Are you still in heat at your age?
SHYLOCK. I say my daughter is my flesh and my blood.

SALARINO. There's more difference between your flesh and hers than between jet and ivory; more between your bloods than there is between red wine and Rhenish. But tell us, have you heard whether Antonio has had any loss at sea or not?

SHYLOCK. There I have another bad match: a bankrupt, a prodigal, who dares scarcely show his head on the Rialto, a beggar who used to come so smug upon the market. Let him look to his bond. He used to call me usurer—let him look to his bond. He used to lend money out of Christian courtesy—let him look to his bond.
SALARINO. Why, I'm sure if he forfeits, you won't take his flesh! What's that good for?

SHYLOCK. To bait fish with. If it feeds nothing else, it will feed my revenge. He has disgraced me, and cost me half a million, laughed at my losses, mocked at my gains, scorned my nation, thwarted my deals, cooled my friends, heated my enemies. And what's his reason? I am a Jew. Has not a Jew eyes? Has not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions? Fed with the same food, hurt by the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same means, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer as a Christian is? If you prick us, do we not bleed? If you tickle us, do we not laugh? If you poison us, do we not die? And if you wrong us, shall we not revenge? If we are like you in the rest, we will resemble you in that. If a Jew wrongs a Christian, what is his humility? Revenge. If a Christian wrongs a Jew, what should his forbearance be, by Christian example? Why, revenge! The villainy you teach me I will execute—and it shall go hard but I will improve on the instruction.
[Enter a man from Antonio.]
SERVANT. Gentlemen, my master Antonio is at his house, and wishes to speak with you both.
SALARINO. We've been up and down looking for him.
[Enter Tubal.]
SOLANIO. Here comes another of the tribe—a third one can't be matched, unless the devil himself turn Jew.
[Exit Solanio, Salarino and the Servant.]
SHYLOCK. How now, Tubal, what news from Genoa? Have you found my daughter?
TUBAL. I often came where I heard of her, but couldn't find her.

SHYLOCK. Why there, there, there, there! A diamond gone that cost me two thousand ducats in Frankfurt! The curse never fell upon our nation until now—I never felt it until now. Two thousand ducats in that, and other precious, precious jewels. I wish my daughter were dead at my foot, and the jewels in her ear; would she were hearsed at my foot, and the ducats in her coffin. No news of them? Why so? And I don't even know what's been spent in the search. Why, you—loss upon loss! The thief gone with so much, and so much to find the thief, and no satisfaction, no revenge, no ill luck stirring but what lights on my shoulders, no sighs but my breathing, no tears but my shedding.
TUBAL. Yes, other men have ill luck too. Antonio, as I heard in Genoa—
SHYLOCK. What, what, what? Ill luck, ill luck?
TUBAL. —had a merchant ship lost coming from Tripoli.
SHYLOCK. I thank God! I thank God! Is it true, is it true?
TUBAL. I spoke with some of the sailors who escaped the wreck.
SHYLOCK. I thank you, good Tubal. Good news, good news! Ha, ha—heard in Genoa?
TUBAL. Your daughter spent, as I heard, in Genoa, in one night, eighty ducats.
SHYLOCK. You stick a dagger in me. I'll never see my gold again. Eighty ducats at one sitting! Eighty ducats!
TUBAL. There came several of Antonio's creditors in my company to Venice who swear he can't help but go bankrupt.
SHYLOCK. I'm very glad of it. I'll plague him, I'll torture him. I'm glad of it.
TUBAL. One of them showed me a ring that he had from your daughter in exchange for a monkey.
SHYLOCK. Out on her! You torture me, Tubal. It was my turquoise—I got it from Leah when I was a bachelor. I wouldn't have given it for a whole wilderness of monkeys.
TUBAL. But Antonio is certainly ruined.

SHYLOCK. Nay, that's true, that's very true. Go, Tubal, hire me an officer—engage him a fortnight in advance. I will have the heart of him if he forfeits—because once he's out of Venice, I can make whatever deals I want. Go, Tubal, and meet me at our synagogue. Go, good Tubal, at our synagogue, Tubal.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — Belmont. A room in Portia’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Bassanio, Portia, Gratiano, Nerissa and all their trains.]

PORTIA. Please wait, pause a day or two before you take the risk—because if you choose wrong, I lose your company. So hold off a while. Something tells me (though it isn't love) that I don't want to lose you, and you know yourself that hatred doesn't counsel in that way. But in case you don't understand me well—and yet a maiden has no tongue but her thoughts—I would keep you here a month or two before you venture for me. I could teach you how to choose right, but then I'd be breaking my oath. I'll never do that. So you may miss me. But if you do, you'll make me wish a sin—that I had broken my oath. Curse your eyes! They have looked me over and divided me. One half of me is yours, the other half yours—mine own, I would say; but if mine, then yours, and so all yours. Oh, these wicked times put bars between owners and their rights! And so though I'm yours, I'm not yours. If it turns out so, let Fortune go to hell for it, not I. I speak too long, but it's to stretch the time, eke it out, draw it out in length, to keep you from making your choice.
BASSANIO. Let me choose, because as things stand I live on the rack.
PORTIA. On the rack, Bassanio? Then confess what treason there is mingled with your love.
BASSANIO. None except that ugly treason of mistrust, which makes me fear I won't get to enjoy my love. There may as well be friendship and life between snow and fire as treason and my love.
PORTIA. Yes, but I fear you speak on the rack, where men under torture will say anything.
BASSANIO. Promise me life, and I'll confess the truth.
PORTIA. Well then, confess and live.
BASSANIO. "Confess and love" would have been the very sum of my confession. Oh, happy torment, when my torturer teaches me the answers for my deliverance! But let me to my fortune and the caskets.

PORTIA. Away then! I'm locked in one of them. If you do love me, you'll find me out. Nerissa and the rest, stand aside, all of you. Let music sound while he makes his choice. Then, if he loses, he makes a swan-like end, fading away in music. To make the comparison more proper, my eye shall be the stream and watery deathbed for him. He may win—and what is music then? Then music is just like the flourish when true subjects bow to a newly crowned monarch. Such it is as those sweet sounds at break of day that creep into the dreaming bridegroom's ear and summon him to marriage. Now he goes, with no less presence, but with much more love, than young Hercules when he rescued the virgin tribute paid by howling Troy to the sea-monster. I stand for the sacrifice; the rest aside are the Trojan wives, with tear-stained faces come out to view the outcome of the exploit. Go, Hercules! If you live, I live. With much, much more dismay I view the fight than you who make the fray.
[A song, whilst Bassanio comments on the caskets to himself.]

Tell me where is fancy bred, / Or in the heart or in the head? / How begot, how nourished? / Reply, reply. / It is engendered in the eyes, / With gazing fed, and fancy dies / In the cradle where it lies. / Let us all ring fancy's knell: / I'll begin it.—Ding, dong, bell.
ALL. Ding, dong, bell.

BASSANIO. So outward shows may be the least like themselves. The world is still deceived with ornament. In law, what plea so tainted and corrupt that, being seasoned with a graceful voice, doesn't obscure the appearance of evil? In religion, what damned error, but some sober brow will bless it, and approve it with a text, hiding the grossness with fair ornament? There's no vice so simple that it doesn't assume some mark of virtue on its outward parts. How many cowards, whose hearts are as false as staircases of sand, still wear upon their chins the beards of Hercules and frowning Mars—who, inwardly examined, have livers white as milk—and these put on the mere outward show of valor to make themselves feared. Look on beauty, and you'll see it's bought by weight, which therein works a miracle in nature, making them lightest who wear most of it. So those curled snaky golden locks which make such wanton play with the wind upon supposed fairness, are often known to be the dowry of a second head—the skull that bred them lying in the sepulchre. Thus ornament is just the deceptive shore to a most dangerous sea; the beautiful scarf veiling an Indian beauty; in a word, the seeming truth which cunning times put on to entrap the wisest. Therefore, you gaudy gold, hard food for Midas, I'll have none of you. Nor any of you, pale and common drudge between man and man. But you, you meager lead, which threatens rather than promises anything—your paleness moves me more than eloquence, and here I choose. Joy be the consequence!
PORTIA.
[Aside.] How all the other passions fly to air—

as doubtful thoughts, and rash-embraced despair, and shuddering fear, and green-eyed jealousy. Oh love, be moderate; calm your ecstasy. In measure rain your joy; restrain this excess! I feel too much of your blessing—make it less, for fear I'm overwhelmed.

BASSANIO. What do I find here? [Opening the leaden casket.] Fair Portia's likeness! What demi-god has come so near to creation? Do these eyes move? Or, riding on the balls of mine, do they only seem in motion? Here are parted lips, separated by sugared breath—so sweet a barrier should ever sunder such sweet friends. Here in her hair the painter plays the spider, and has woven a golden mesh to trap the hearts of men faster than gnats in cobwebs. But her eyes!—how could he see to do them? Having made one, I'd think it should have power to steal both of his own and leave itself unfinished. Yet look how far the substance of my praise wrongs this shadow by underprizing it, just so far does this shadow limp behind the substance. Here's the scroll, the content and summary of my fortune.

You that choose not by the sight, / Chance as fair, and choose as right! / Since this fortune falls to you, / Be content and seek no new. / If you be well pleased with this, / And hold your fortune for your bliss, / Turn to where your lady is, / And claim her with a loving kiss.

A gentle scroll. Fair lady, by your leave, [Kissing her,] I come by directive to give and to receive. Like one of two contending in a contest, who thinks he has done well in people's eyes, hearing applause and universal shout, giddy in spirit, still gazing in doubt whether those peals of praise are his or not—so, thrice-fair lady, I stand the same way, doubtful whether what I see is true, until confirmed, signed, ratified by you.

PORTIA. You see me, Lord Bassanio, where I stand, such as I am. Though for myself alone I would not be ambitious in my wish to wish myself much better, yet for you I would be trebled twenty times myself, a thousand times more fair, ten thousand times more rich—that only to stand high in your account, I might in virtues, beauties, livings, friends, exceed accounting. But the full sum of me is the sum of something which, to put in gross terms, is an untaught girl, unschooled, unpracticed. Happy in this, she's not yet so old but she may learn; happier than this, she's not bred so dull but she can learn; happiest of all, her gentle spirit commits itself to yours to be directed, as by her lord, her governor, her king. Myself and what is mine, to you and yours is now converted. Just now I was the lord of this fair mansion, master of my servants, queen over myself; and even now, but now, this house, these servants, and this very self are yours—my lord's. I give them with this ring, which when you part with, lose, or give away, let it presage the ruin of your love and be my warrant to denounce you.

BASSANIO. Madam, you've left me without words. Only my blood speaks to you in my veins, and there's such confusion in my powers as, after some oration finely spoken by a beloved prince, appears among the buzzing pleased multitude, where every separate something being blended together turns to a wildness of nothing, except of joy expressed and not expressed. But when this ring leaves this finger, then life leaves this body. Oh then be bold to say Bassanio's dead!
NERISSA. My lord and lady, it's now our time—we who've stood by and seen our wishes prosper—to cry, good joy. Good joy, my lord and lady!

GRATIANO. My Lord Bassanio, and my gentle lady, I wish you all the joy you can wish—because I'm sure you can't wish any from me. And when your honors mean to solemnize the bargain of your faith, I beseech you that at that same time I may be married too.
BASSANIO. With all my heart, so long as you can get a wife.

GRATIANO. I thank your lordship, you have got me one. My eyes, my lord, can look as quickly as yours. You saw the mistress, I beheld the maid. You loved, I loved—because pausing applies no more to me, my lord, than to you. Your fortune depended on the caskets there, and so did mine too, as it happens. For wooing here until I sweated again, and swearing till my very roof was dry with oaths of love, at last (if a promise lasts) I got a promise from this fair one here to have her love, provided your fortune secured her mistress.
PORTIA. Is this true, Nerissa?
NERISSA. Madam, it is, if you're pleased with it.
BASSANIO. And do you, Gratiano, mean it in good faith?
GRATIANO. Yes, faith, my lord.
BASSANIO. Our feast shall be much honored by your marriage.
GRATIANO. We'll wager with them the first boy for a thousand ducats.
NERISSA. What! And stake the money down?
GRATIANO. No, we shall never win at that sport with the stake down. But who comes here? Lorenzo and his infidel? What, and my old Venetian friend, Salerio!
[Enter Lorenzo, Jessica and Salerio.]
BASSANIO. Lorenzo and Salerio, welcome here—if the newness of my new authority here has power to bid you welcome. By your leave, I bid my very friends and countrymen, sweet Portia, welcome.
PORTIA. So do I, my lord. They are entirely welcome.
LORENZO. I thank your honor. For my part, my lord, my purpose wasn't to have seen you here, but, meeting with Salerio on the way, he begged me, past all refusal, to come along with him.
SALERIO. I did, my lord, and I have reason for it. Signior Antonio commends himself to you.
[Gives Bassanio a letter.]
BASSANIO. Before I open his letter, please tell me how my good friend is.
SALERIO. Not sick, my lord, unless it be in mind; nor well, unless in mind. His letter there will show you his state.
[Bassanio opens the letter.]

GRATIANO. Nerissa, cheer up the lady stranger—bid her welcome. Your hand, Salerio. What's the news from Venice? How is that royal merchant, good Antonio? I know he'll be glad of our success. We are the Jasons, we have won the fleece.
SALERIO. I wish you had won the fleece that he has lost.

PORTIA. There are some sharp contents in that paper that steal the color from Bassanio's cheek. Some dear friend dead—otherwise nothing in the world could so transform the constitution of any constant man. What, worse and worse? By your leave, Bassanio, I am half yourself, and I must freely have the half of anything this paper brings you.

BASSANIO. Oh sweet Portia, here are a few of the most unpleasant words that ever blotted paper. Gentle lady, when I first revealed my love to you, I freely told you all the wealth I had ran in my veins—I was a gentleman. And then I told you the truth. And yet, dear lady, rating myself at nothing, you shall see how much I was a braggart. When I told you my estate was nothing, I should have told you then that I was worse than nothing. Because indeed I have engaged myself to a dear friend, engaged my friend to his outright enemy, to feed my means. Here is a letter, lady, the paper as the body of my friend, and every word in it a gaping wound issuing life-blood. But is it true, Salerio? Have all his ventures failed? What, not one hit? From Tripoli, from Mexico, and England, from Lisbon, Barbary, and India, and not one vessel escape the dreadful touch of merchant-marring rocks?

SALERIO. Not one, my lord. Besides, it appears that even if he had the money on hand to pay off the Jew, the Jew wouldn't take it. Never have I known a creature that bore the shape of a man so keen and greedy to destroy a man. He badgers the Duke morning and night, and challenges the freedom of the state if they deny him justice. Twenty merchants, the Duke himself, and the most important magnates have all tried to dissuade him, but no one can drive him from his spiteful insistence on the forfeit, on justice, and on his bond.

JESSICA. When I was with him, I heard him swear to Tubal and to Chus, his countrymen, that he'd rather have Antonio's flesh than twenty times the value of the sum he owed him. And I know, my lord, if law, authority, and power do not deny him, it will go hard with poor Antonio.
PORTIA. Is it your dear friend who's thus in trouble?

BASSANIO. The dearest friend to me, the kindest man, the best-natured and most tireless spirit in doing kindnesses, and one in whom the ancient Roman honor appears more than in any man that draws breath in Italy.
PORTIA. What sum does he owe the Jew?
BASSANIO. For me, three thousand ducats.

PORTIA. What, no more? Pay him six thousand, and tear up the bond. Double six thousand, and then treble that, before a friend of this description shall lose a hair through Bassanio's fault. First, go with me to church and call me wife, and then away to Venice to your friend. Because never shall you lie by Portia's side with an unquiet soul. You shall have gold to pay the petty debt twenty times over. When it's paid, bring your true friend along. My maid Nerissa and myself meanwhile will live as maids and widows. Come, away! Because you'll go from here on your wedding day. Bid your friends welcome, show a merry cheer; since you're dearly bought, I will love you dearly. But let me hear the letter from your friend.

BASSANIO. Sweet Bassanio, all my ships have miscarried, my creditors grow cruel, my estate is very low, my bond to the Jew is forfeit, and since in paying it, it's impossible I should live, all debts are cleared between you and me, if I might just see you at my death. Notwithstanding, do as you please. If your love doesn't persuade you to come, don't let my letter.
PORTIA. Oh love, dispatch all business and be gone!
BASSANIO. Since I have your good leave to go away, I'll hurry. But, until I come again, no bed shall ever be guilty of my staying in it, nor shall rest come between us two.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — Venice. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Shylock, Salarino, Antonio and Gaoler.]
SHYLOCK. Jailer, keep an eye on him. Don't talk to me of mercy. This is the fool that lent out money for free. Jailer, keep an eye on him.
ANTONIO. Hear me out, good Shylock.

SHYLOCK. I'll have my bond, speak not against my bond. I've sworn an oath that I will have my bond. You called me dog before you had any cause—but since I am a dog, beware my fangs. The Duke shall grant me justice. I'm amazed, you foolish jailer, that you're so soft as to come out with him at his request.
ANTONIO. Please hear me speak.

SHYLOCK. I'll have my bond. I won't hear you speak. I'll have my bond, so speak no more. I won't be made into a soft and dull-eyed fool, to shake my head, relent, sigh, and yield to Christian intercessors. Don't follow me—I'll have no talking. I will have my bond.
[Exit.]
SALARINO. He's the most impenetrable cur that ever lived among men.

ANTONIO. Let him alone. I'll follow him no more with useless prayers. He seeks my life—I know his reason well. I often delivered from his forfeitures many people who at times came complaining to me. That's why he hates me.
SALARINO. I'm sure the Duke will never let this forfeit stand.

ANTONIO. The Duke cannot deny the course of law, because the trading privileges that foreigners have with us in Venice, if denied, would much impair the justice of the state—since the trade and profit of the city consists of all nations. So go. These griefs and losses have so worn me down that I'll hardly be able to spare a pound of flesh tomorrow for my bloody creditor. Well, jailer, on—pray God Bassanio comes to see me pay his debt, and then I won't mind.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 4 — Belmont. A room in Portia’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Portia, Nerissa, Lorenzo, Jessica and Balthazar.]

LORENZO. Madam, though I say it in your presence, you have a noble and true understanding of godlike friendship, which shows most strongly in your bearing the absence of your lord this way. But if you knew to whom you're showing this honor, how true a gentleman you're sending relief to, how dear a friend to my lord your husband, I know you'd be prouder of the work than customary generosity can compel you to be.

PORTIA. I've never repented doing good, and I won't now. For in companions who keep company and spend time together, whose souls bear an equal yoke of love, there must be a like proportion of features, manners, and spirit. Which makes me think that this Antonio, being the bosom friend of my lord, must necessarily be like my lord. If that's so, how small is the cost I've laid out to purchase the likeness of my own soul from a state of hellish cruelty! This comes too near praising myself, so no more of it. Hear other matters. Lorenzo, I commit into your hands the management and running of my house until my lord's return. For my own part, I've breathed toward heaven a secret vow to live in prayer and contemplation, attended only by Nerissa here, until her husband and my lord return. There's a monastery two miles off, and there we'll stay. I beg you not to refuse this charge, which my love and some necessity now lay upon you.
LORENZO. Madam, with all my heart I shall obey you in all fair commands.
PORTIA. My household already knows my mind, and will acknowledge you and Jessica in place of Lord Bassanio and myself. So fare you well till we meet again.
LORENZO. May fair thoughts and happy hours attend you!
JESSICA. I wish your ladyship all heart's content.
PORTIA. I thank you for your wish, and am well pleased to wish it back on you. Fare you well, Jessica.
[Exit Jessica and Lorenzo.]

Now, Balthazar, since I've always found you honest-true, let me find you still so. Take this letter and use all the endeavor of a man in speeding to Padua. See that you deliver this into my cousin's hands, Doctor Bellario. And whatever notes and garments he gives you, bring them, please, with imagined speed to the ferry-crossing, the common ferry that trades to Venice. Waste no time in words—just get going. I'll be there before you.
BALTHAZAR. Madam, I go with all suitable speed.
[Exit.]
PORTIA. Come on, Nerissa, I have work in hand that you don't yet know about. We'll see our husbands before they think of us.
NERISSA. Will they see us?

PORTIA. They shall, Nerissa, but in such a get-up that they'll think we are equipped with what we lack. I'll bet you anything—when we're both outfitted like young men, I'll prove the prettier fellow of the two, and wear my dagger with a braver grace, and speak between the change of man and boy with a reedy voice; and turn two mincing steps into a manly stride; and speak of frays like a fine bragging youth; and tell quaint lies—how honorable ladies sought my love, which I denied, and they fell sick and died, I couldn't help it. Then I'll repent, and wish, for all that, that I hadn't killed them. And twenty of these puny lies I'll tell, that men shall swear I've been out of school for about a year. I have within my mind a thousand raw tricks of these bragging Jacks, which I'll practice.
NERISSA. Why, are we going to turn into men?
