PORTIA. Fie, what a question that is, if you were near a lewd interpreter! But come, I'll tell you my whole plan when I'm in my coach, which is waiting for us at the park gate. So hurry away—we must cover twenty miles today.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 5 — The same. A garden
paragraphs: [Enter Launcelet and Jessica.]

LAUNCELET. Yes, truly—because, look you, the sins of the father are to be laid upon the children. Therefore, I promise you, I fear for you. I was always plain with you, and so now I speak my agitation about the matter. Therefore be of good cheer, because truly I think you're damned. There's just one hope in it that can do you any good, and that's only a kind of bastard hope at that.
JESSICA. And what hope is that, please?
LAUNCELET. Marry, you may partly hope that your father didn't sire you—that you're not the Jew's daughter.
JESSICA. That would be a kind of bastard hope indeed; so the sins of my mother would be visited upon me.
LAUNCELET. Truly then I fear you're damned both by father and mother. Thus when I avoid Scylla your father, I fall into Charybdis your mother. Well, you're gone both ways.
JESSICA. I shall be saved by my husband. He's made me a Christian.

LAUNCELET. Truly, the more to blame he—we were Christians enough before, just as many as could well live one alongside another. This making of Christians will raise the price of hogs. If we all become pork-eaters, soon we won't have a rasher on the coals for any money.
[Enter Lorenzo.]
JESSICA. I'll tell my husband, Launcelet, what you say. Here he comes.
LORENZO. I shall grow jealous of you shortly, Launcelet, if you keep getting my wife into corners like this!

JESSICA. No, you needn't worry about us, Lorenzo. Launcelet and I are at odds. He tells me flatly there's no mercy for me in heaven, because I'm a Jew's daughter—and he says you're no good member of the commonwealth, because in converting Jews to Christians you raise the price of pork.
LORENZO. I shall answer that better to the commonwealth than you can answer for the swelling of the Moorish woman's belly! The Moor is with child by you, Launcelet.
LAUNCELET. It is much that the Moor should be more than reason; but if she be less than an honest woman, she is indeed more than I took her for.

LORENZO. How every fool can play with words! I think the best grace of wit will shortly turn into silence, and conversation will be commendable in none but parrots. Go inside, sirrah—tell them to prepare for dinner.
LAUNCELET. That's already done, sir—they all have stomachs.
LORENZO. Goodly Lord, what a wit-snapper you are! Then bid them prepare dinner.
LAUNCELET. That's done too, sir—"cover" is the word now.
LORENZO. Will you cover, then, sir?
LAUNCELET. Not so, sir, neither. I know my duty.

LORENZO. More quibbling with the occasion! Will you show the whole wealth of your wit in an instant? Please understand a plain man in his plain meaning: go to your fellows, tell them to cover the table, serve in the meat, and we'll come in to dinner.
LAUNCELET. For the table, sir, it shall be served in; for the meat, sir, it shall be covered; for your coming in to dinner, sir, why, let it be as moods and fancies shall govern.
[Exit.]

LORENZO. Oh dear discretion, how his words are suited! The fool has planted in his memory an army of good words, and I know many fools who stand in better positions, decked out like him, who for a tricky word defy the matter. How cheer you, Jessica? And now, good sweet, give me your opinion—how do you like Lord Bassanio's wife?

JESSICA. Beyond all expressing. It's very right that Lord Bassanio live an upright life, since having such a blessing in his lady, he finds the joys of heaven here on earth—and if on earth he doesn't deserve it, in reason he should never come to heaven. Why, if two gods should play some heavenly match, and on the wager lay two earthly women, with Portia one of them, there must be something else added on the other side, because the poor crude world doesn't have her equal.
LORENZO. Just such a husband have you in me as she is for a wife.
JESSICA. No, but ask my opinion of that too.
LORENZO. I will in a moment. First let's go to dinner.
JESSICA. No, let me praise you while I still have appetite.
LORENZO. No, please, save it for table-talk. Then however you speak, among other things, I shall digest it.
JESSICA. Well, I'll lay out your praises.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — Venice. A court of justice
paragraphs: [Enter the Duke, the Magnificoes, Antonio, Bassanio, Gratiano, Salerio and others.]
DUKE. What, is Antonio here?
ANTONIO. Ready, if it please your Grace.
DUKE. I am sorry for you—you've come to answer a stony adversary, an inhuman wretch, incapable of pity, void and empty of any drop of mercy.

ANTONIO. I've heard your Grace has taken great pains to soften his rigorous course. But since he remains obdurate, and no lawful means can carry me out of the reach of his malice, I oppose my patience to his fury, and am armed to suffer with a quietness of spirit the very tyranny and rage he can bring.
DUKE. Someone go and call the Jew into the court.
SALARINO. He's ready at the door. He's coming, my lord.
[Enter Shylock.]

DUKE. Make room, and let him stand before us. Shylock, the world thinks, and I think so too, that you keep up this show of malice only to the last hour of the matter, and then, it's thought, you'll show your mercy and remorse more strange than your strange apparent cruelty. And where you now exact the penalty—which is a pound of this poor merchant's flesh—you'll not only loose the forfeit, but, touched with human gentleness and love, forgive a portion of the principal, glancing an eye of pity on his losses, which have lately so piled on his back as to press a royal merchant down and pluck commiseration of his state from brassy bosoms and rough flint hearts, from stubborn Turks and Tartars never trained to offices of tender courtesy. We all expect a gentle answer, Jew.

SHYLOCK. I have informed your Grace of what I intend, and by our holy Sabbath I have sworn to have the due forfeit of my bond. If you deny it, let the danger fall upon your charter and your city's freedom! You'll ask me why I'd rather have a weight of carrion flesh than receive three thousand ducats. I won't answer that—but say it's my mood. Is that answered? What if my house is troubled with a rat, and I'm pleased to give ten thousand ducats to have it killed? What, are you answered yet? Some men there are who don't love a roast pig with its mouth open. Some who go mad at the sight of a cat. And others, when the bagpipe sings in the nose, can't hold their urine—because emotion, mistress of passion, sways it to the mood of what it likes or loathes. Now, for your answer: just as no firm reason can be given why one man can't stand a gaping pig, why another can't bear a harmless necessary cat, why another can't endure a woolen bagpipe—but must, by force, yield to such inevitable shame as to offend, being himself offended—so I can give no reason, nor will I, beyond a lodged hatred and a certain loathing I bear Antonio, that I pursue this losing suit against him. Are you answered?
BASSANIO. This is no answer, you unfeeling man, to excuse the current of your cruelty.
SHYLOCK. I'm not obligated to please you with my answer.
BASSANIO. Do all men kill the things they don't love?
SHYLOCK. Does any man hate the thing he wouldn't kill?
BASSANIO. Every offense is not a hate at first.
SHYLOCK. What, would you have a serpent sting you twice?

ANTONIO. Please, consider that you're arguing with the Jew. You may as well go stand on the beach and order the high tide to lower its usual height. You may as well argue with the wolf about why he's made the ewe bleat for the lamb. You may as well forbid the mountain pines to wag their high tops and make no noise when they're fretted with the gusts of heaven. You may as well do anything most hard as seek to soften that—and what's harder than this?—his Jewish heart. So I beg you, make no more offers, use no further means—but with all brief and plain dispatch, let me have judgment, and the Jew his will.
BASSANIO. For your three thousand ducats here is six.
SHYLOCK. If every ducat in six thousand ducats were in six parts, and every part a ducat, I wouldn't take them—I would have my bond.
DUKE. How will you hope for mercy, rendering none?

SHYLOCK. What judgment shall I dread, doing no wrong? You have among you many a purchased slave, which, like your asses and your dogs and mules, you use in abject and slavish jobs, because you bought them. Shall I say to you, "Let them be free, marry them to your heirs? Why do they sweat under burdens? Let their beds be made as soft as yours, and let their palates be seasoned with such viands"? You'll answer, "The slaves are ours." So I answer you: the pound of flesh I demand of him is dearly bought; it's mine and I will have it. If you deny me, fie upon your law! There's no force in the decrees of Venice. I stand for judgment. Answer: shall I have it?
DUKE. By my power I may dismiss this court, unless Bellario, a learned doctor, whom I've sent for to determine this, comes here today.
SALARINO. My lord, there waits outside a messenger with letters from the doctor, just come from Padua.
DUKE. Bring us the letters. Call the messenger.
BASSANIO. Cheer up, Antonio! What, man, courage yet! The Jew shall have my flesh, blood, bones, and all, before you lose for me one drop of blood.

ANTONIO. I am a diseased ram of the flock, fittest for death. The weakest kind of fruit drops earliest to the ground, and so let me. You can't be better employed, Bassanio, than to live still, and write my epitaph.
[Enter Nerissa dressed like a lawyer's clerk.]
DUKE. Did you come from Padua, from Bellario?
NERISSA. From both, my lord. Bellario greets your Grace.
[Presents a letter.]
BASSANIO. Why do you whet your knife so earnestly?
SHYLOCK. To cut the forfeit from that bankrupt there.
GRATIANO. Not on your sole but on your soul, harsh Jew, you sharpen your knife. But no metal can—no, not the hangman's axe—bear half the keenness of your sharp malice. Can no prayers pierce you?
SHYLOCK. No, none that you have the wit to make.

GRATIANO. Oh, be damned, inexorable dog! And for your life let justice be blamed. You almost make me waver in my faith, to hold the opinion of Pythagoras that souls of animals infuse themselves into the bodies of men. Your currish spirit governed a wolf who, hanged for human slaughter, even from the gallows had his cruel soul flee away, and while you lay in your unhallowed mother, infused itself into you. Because your desires are wolfish, bloody, starved, and ravenous.
SHYLOCK. Until you can rail the seal from off my bond, you only injure your lungs to speak so loud. Repair your wit, good youth, or it will fall to cureless ruin. I stand here for law.
DUKE. This letter from Bellario commends a young and learned doctor to our court. Where is he?
NERISSA. He's attending here nearby, to know your answer—whether you'll admit him.
DUKE OF VENICE. With all my heart. Some three or four of you, go give him courteous escort to this place. Meanwhile, the court shall hear Bellario's letter.
[Reads.] Your Grace shall understand that on receipt of your

letter I am very sick. But at the very moment your messenger arrived, in loving visitation was with me a young doctor of Rome. His name is Balthazar. I acquainted him with the cause in dispute between the Jew and Antonio the merchant. We turned over many books together. He is furnished with my opinion, which, bettered with his own learning (the greatness of which I cannot praise enough), comes with him at my urging to fill up your Grace's request in my stead. I beseech you, let his lack of years be no impediment to a reverend estimation of him, because I never knew so young a body with so old a head. I leave him to your gracious acceptance, whose trial shall better publish his commendation.
You hear what the learned Bellario writes, and here, I take it, is the doctor come.
[Enter Portia dressed like a doctor of laws.]
Give me your hand. Did you come from old Bellario?
PORTIA. I did, my lord.
DUKE. You are welcome. Take your place. Are you acquainted with the dispute that holds this present question in the court?
PORTIA. I am thoroughly informed of the case. Which is the merchant here? And which the Jew?
DUKE. Antonio and old Shylock, both step forward.
PORTIA. Is your name Shylock?
SHYLOCK. Shylock is my name.
PORTIA. Of a strange nature is the suit you're pursuing—yet so much within the rules that Venetian law cannot challenge you as you proceed.
[To Antonio.] You stand within his danger, do you not?
ANTONIO. Yes, so he says.
PORTIA. Do you confess the bond?
ANTONIO. I do.
PORTIA. Then must the Jew be merciful.
SHYLOCK. On what compulsion must I? Tell me that.

PORTIA. The quality of mercy is not strained. It drops as the gentle rain from heaven upon the place beneath. It is twice blessed: it blesses him that gives and him that takes. 'Tis mightiest in the mightiest. It becomes the throned monarch better than his crown. His scepter shows the force of temporal power, the attribute of awe and majesty, wherein sits the dread and fear of kings. But mercy is above this sceptered sway. It is enthroned in the hearts of kings. It is an attribute of God himself, and earthly power then shows likest God's when mercy seasons justice. Therefore, Jew, though justice be your plea, consider this: that in the course of justice, none of us should see salvation. We do pray for mercy, and that same prayer teaches us all to render the deeds of mercy. I have spoken thus much to mitigate the justice of your plea—which if you pursue, this strict court of Venice must give sentence against the merchant there.
SHYLOCK. My deeds upon my head! I crave the law, the penalty and forfeit of my bond.
PORTIA. Is he not able to pay the money?

BASSANIO. Yes, here I tender it for him in the court—indeed, twice the sum. If that won't suffice, I'll be bound to pay it ten times over, on forfeit of my hands, my head, my heart. If this won't suffice, it must be clear that malice bears down truth. And I beseech you—just once, bend the law to your authority. To do a great right, do a little wrong, and curb this cruel devil of his will.
PORTIA. It must not be. There's no power in Venice can alter an established decree. It would be recorded as a precedent, and many an error by the same example would rush into the state. It cannot be.
SHYLOCK. A Daniel come to judgment! Yes, a Daniel! Oh wise young judge, how I honor you!
PORTIA. Please let me look at the bond.
SHYLOCK. Here it is, most reverend doctor, here it is.
PORTIA. Shylock, there's thrice your money offered to you.
SHYLOCK. An oath, an oath! I have an oath in heaven. Shall I lay perjury upon my soul? No, not for Venice.

PORTIA. Why, this bond is forfeit, and lawfully by this the Jew may claim a pound of flesh, to be cut by him off nearest the merchant's heart. Be merciful—take thrice your money; tell me to tear up the bond.

SHYLOCK. When it is paid according to its terms. It appears that you are a worthy judge. You know the law; your interpretation has been most sound. I charge you by the law, of which you are a well-deserving pillar, to proceed to judgment. By my soul I swear there is no power in the tongue of man to alter me. I stand here on my bond.
ANTONIO. Most heartily I beseech the court to give the judgment.
PORTIA. Why then, thus it is: you must prepare your bosom for his knife.
SHYLOCK. Oh noble judge! Oh excellent young man!
PORTIA. Because the intent and purpose of the law has full relation to the penalty, which here appears due upon the bond.
SHYLOCK. It is very true. Oh wise and upright judge, how much more elder you are than your looks!
PORTIA. Therefore lay bare your bosom.
SHYLOCK. Yes, his breast. So says the bond, doesn't it, noble judge? "Nearest his heart"—those are the very words.
PORTIA. It is so. Are there scales here to weigh the flesh?
SHYLOCK. I have them ready.
PORTIA. Have a surgeon here, Shylock, at your charge, to stop his wounds, lest he bleed to death.
SHYLOCK. Is it so named in the bond?
PORTIA. It is not expressly stated, but what of that? It would be good if you did so much for charity.
SHYLOCK. I can't find it; it's not in the bond.
PORTIA. You, merchant, have you anything to say?

ANTONIO. But little. I am armed and well prepared. Give me your hand, Bassanio. Fare you well. Don't grieve that I've fallen to this for you, because here Fortune shows herself more kind than is her custom. It is usually her way to let the wretched man outlive his wealth, to view with hollow eye and wrinkled brow an age of poverty—from which lingering penance of such misery she cuts me off. Commend me to your honorable wife. Tell her the manner of Antonio's end. Say how I loved you, speak fair of me in death. And when the tale is told, ask her to judge whether Bassanio had not once a love. Only repent that you'll lose your friend, and he doesn't repent that he pays your debt. Because if the Jew only cuts deep enough, I'll pay it instantly with all my heart.

BASSANIO. Antonio, I am married to a wife who is as dear to me as life itself. But life itself, my wife, and all the world are not, in my eyes, valued above your life. I would lose everything—yes, sacrifice them all here to this devil—to deliver you.
PORTIA. Your wife would give you little thanks for that if she were here to hear you make the offer.
GRATIANO. I have a wife who, I swear, I love. I wish she were in heaven, so she could beg some power to change this currish Jew.
NERISSA. It's just as well you offer it behind her back—otherwise the wish would make an unquiet house.
SHYLOCK. These are the Christian husbands! I have a daughter—I wish any of the stock of Barabbas had been her husband, rather than a Christian! We waste time—please, pursue sentence.
PORTIA. A pound of that same merchant's flesh is yours. The court awards it and the law gives it.
SHYLOCK. Most rightful judge!
PORTIA. And you must cut this flesh from off his breast. The law allows it and the court awards it.
SHYLOCK. Most learned judge! A sentence! Come, prepare.

PORTIA. Wait a little—there is something else. This bond gives you here not a jot of blood. The words are expressly "a pound of flesh". Take then your bond, take your pound of flesh. But in cutting it, if you shed one drop of Christian blood, your lands and goods are, by the laws of Venice, confiscated to the state of Venice.
GRATIANO. Oh upright judge! Mark that, Jew. Oh learned judge!
SHYLOCK. Is that the law?
PORTIA. You yourself shall see the statute. Because, as you urge justice, be assured you shall have justice more than you desire.
GRATIANO. Oh learned judge! Mark that, Jew, a learned judge!
SHYLOCK. I'll take this offer then. Pay the bond three times over and let the Christian go.
BASSANIO. Here is the money.
PORTIA. Wait! The Jew shall have all justice. Wait! No haste! He shall have nothing but the penalty.
GRATIANO. Oh Jew, an upright judge, a learned judge!

PORTIA. Therefore prepare yourself to cut off the flesh. Shed no blood, nor cut less nor more, but just a pound of flesh. If you take more or less than a just pound—be it but so much as makes it light or heavy in substance, or the division of the twentieth part of one poor scruple—nay, if the scale turns but by the estimation of a hair, you die, and all your goods are confiscated.
GRATIANO. A second Daniel, a Daniel, Jew! Now, infidel, I have you on the hip.
PORTIA. Why does the Jew pause? Take your forfeit.
SHYLOCK. Give me my principal, and let me go.
BASSANIO. I have it ready for you. Here it is.
PORTIA. He has refused it in the open court. He shall have nothing but justice, and his bond.
GRATIANO. A Daniel still I say, a second Daniel! I thank you, Jew, for teaching me that word.
SHYLOCK. Shall I not have just my principal?
PORTIA. You shall have nothing but the forfeit, to be so taken at your peril, Jew.
SHYLOCK. Why then, the devil give him good of it! I'll stay no longer to argue.

PORTIA. Wait, Jew. The law has yet another hold on you. It is enacted in the laws of Venice that if it be proved against an alien that by direct or indirect attempts he seeks the life of any citizen, the party against whom he contrives shall seize one half of his goods. The other half goes to the privy coffer of the state. And the offender's life lies in the mercy of the Duke alone, against all other voice. In which predicament I say you stand. For it appears by manifest proceeding that indirectly, and directly too, you have contrived against the very life of the defendant. And you have incurred the danger I formerly rehearsed. Down, therefore, and beg mercy of the Duke.

GRATIANO. Beg that you may have leave to hang yourself. And yet, since your wealth is forfeit to the state, you don't have left the value of a cord—therefore you must be hanged at the state's expense.

DUKE. So that you shall see the difference of our spirit, I pardon you your life before you ask it. As for half your wealth, it is Antonio's. The other half comes to the general state, which humbleness may reduce to a fine.
PORTIA. Yes, for the state, not for Antonio.
SHYLOCK. No, take my life and all, don't pardon that. You take my house when you take the prop that sustains my house. You take my life when you take the means by which I live.
PORTIA. What mercy can you render him, Antonio?
GRATIANO. A noose free of charge, nothing else, for God's sake!

ANTONIO. If it please my lord the Duke and all the court to drop the fine for one half of his goods, I am content—so long as he'll let me have the other half in trust, to render it upon his death to the gentleman who lately stole his daughter. Two more conditions: that, for this favor, he immediately become a Christian; the other, that he record a gift, here in the court, of everything he dies possessing, to his son Lorenzo and his daughter.
DUKE. He shall do this, or else I retract the pardon I just pronounced here.
PORTIA. Are you contented, Jew? What do you say?
SHYLOCK. I am content.
PORTIA. Clerk, draw a deed of gift.
SHYLOCK. Please give me leave to go from here. I am not well. Send the deed after me and I will sign it.
DUKE. Get you gone, but do it.
GRATIANO. At your christening you shall have two godfathers. Had I been judge, you would have had ten more—to bring you to the gallows, not to the font.
[Exit Shylock.]
DUKE. Sir, I entreat you home with me to dinner.
PORTIA. I humbly beg your Grace's pardon. I must away this night toward Padua, and it's right that I set out at once.
DUKE. I'm sorry that your leisure doesn't permit it. Antonio, reward this gentleman, for in my mind you are much bound to him.
[Exit Duke and his train.]

BASSANIO. Most worthy gentleman, I and my friend have by your wisdom been this day acquitted of grievous penalties—in lieu of which, three thousand ducats due unto the Jew we freely offer in payment of your courteous pains.
ANTONIO. And remain indebted, over and above, in love and service to you evermore.

PORTIA. He is well paid that is well satisfied. And I, delivering you, am satisfied, and therein account myself well paid. My mind was never yet more mercenary. Please know me when we meet again. I wish you well, and so I take my leave.
BASSANIO. Dear sir, of necessity I must press you further. Take some remembrance of us as a tribute, not as a fee. Grant me two things, please: not to deny me, and to pardon me.
PORTIA. You press me far, and therefore I'll yield.
[To Antonio.] Give me your gloves, I'll wear them for your sake.
[To Bassanio.] And, for your love, I'll take this ring from you.
Don't draw back your hand—I'll take no more, and you in love shall not deny me this.
BASSANIO. This ring, good sir? Alas, it is a trifle. I won't shame myself to give you this.
PORTIA. I will have nothing else but only this, and now I think I have a mind to it.
BASSANIO. There's more depends on this than on the value. The dearest ring in Venice will I give you—I'll find it out by proclamation. Only for this, please pardon me.
PORTIA. I see, sir, you are generous with offers. You taught me first to beg, and now I think you teach me how a beggar should be answered.
BASSANIO. Good sir, this ring was given me by my wife, and when she put it on, she made me vow that I should neither sell, nor give, nor lose it.

PORTIA. That excuse serves many men to save their gifts. And if your wife isn't a madwoman, and knows how well I have deserved this ring, she wouldn't hold out as your enemy forever for giving it to me. Well, peace be with you!
[Exit Portia and Nerissa.]
ANTONIO. My Lord Bassanio, let him have the ring. Let his deservings and my love along with it be weighed against your wife's command.
BASSANIO. Go, Gratiano, run and overtake him. Give him the ring, and bring him, if you can, to Antonio's house. Away, make haste.
[Exit Gratiano.]
Come, you and I will go there at once, and in the morning early we'll both fly toward Belmont. Come, Antonio.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — The same. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Portia and Nerissa.]
PORTIA. Find out the Jew's house, give him this deed, and have him sign it. We'll be away tonight, and be home a day before our husbands. This deed will be very welcome to Lorenzo.
[Enter Gratiano.]
GRATIANO. Fair sir, you're well caught up with. My Lord Bassanio on further thought has sent you this ring here, and entreats your company at dinner.
PORTIA. That can't be. His ring I do accept most thankfully—please tell him so. Furthermore, please show my young clerk to old Shylock's house.
GRATIANO. That I will do.
NERISSA. Sir, I'd like to speak with you.
[Aside to Portia.]
I'll see if I can get my husband's ring, which I made him swear to keep forever.
PORTIA.
[To Nerissa.] You may, I warrant. We shall have old swearing
that they gave the rings away to men. But we'll outface them, and outswear them too. Away! Make haste! You know where I'll wait.
NERISSA. Come, good sir, will you show me to this house?
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Belmont. The avenue to Portia’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Lorenzo and Jessica.]

LORENZO. The moon shines bright. On a night like this, when the sweet wind gently kissed the trees, and they made no noise—on such a night, I think, Troilus mounted the Trojan walls and sighed his soul toward the Grecian tents where Cressid lay that night.
JESSICA. On such a night Thisbe fearfully tripped over the dew, and saw the lion's shadow before the lion itself, and ran away dismayed.
LORENZO. On such a night Dido stood with a willow in her hand upon the wild sea-banks, and waved her love to come again to Carthage.
JESSICA. On such a night Medea gathered the enchanted herbs that renewed old Aeson.
LORENZO. On such a night Jessica stole away from the wealthy Jew, and with a spendthrift love ran from Venice as far as Belmont.
JESSICA. On such a night young Lorenzo swore he loved her well, stealing her soul with many vows of faith, and never a true one.
LORENZO. On such a night pretty Jessica, like a little shrew, slandered her love, and he forgave it her.
JESSICA. I would out-night you if nobody came; but listen, I hear a man's footsteps.
[Enter Stephano.]
LORENZO. Who comes so fast in the silence of the night?
STEPHANO. A friend.
LORENZO. A friend! What friend? Your name, please, friend?
STEPHANO. Stephano is my name, and I bring word that my mistress will be here at Belmont before daybreak. She is wandering by holy crosses where she kneels and prays for happy wedlock hours.
LORENZO. Who comes with her?
STEPHANO. None but a holy hermit and her maid. Please, has my master returned yet?
LORENZO. He has not, nor have we heard from him. But let's go in, please, Jessica, and ceremoniously prepare some welcome for the mistress of the house.
[Enter Launcelet.]
LAUNCELET. Sola, sola! Wo ha, ho! Sola, sola!
LORENZO. Who calls?
LAUNCELET. Sola! Did you see Master Lorenzo? Master Lorenzo! Sola, sola!
LORENZO. Stop hollering, man. Here!
LAUNCELET. Sola! Where, where?
LORENZO. Here!
LAUNCELET. Tell him there's a courier come from my master with his horn full of good news. My master will be here before morning.
[Exit.]

LORENZO. Sweet soul, let's go in, and there expect their coming. And yet no matter—why should we go in? My friend Stephano, please go inside the house and let them know your mistress is at hand, and bring your musicians forth into the open air.
[Exit Stephano.]

How sweet the moonlight sleeps upon this bank! Here we'll sit and let the sounds of music creep into our ears. Soft stillness and the night become the touches of sweet harmony. Sit, Jessica. Look how the floor of heaven is thickly inlaid with discs of bright gold. There's not the smallest sphere you see but in its motion sings like an angel, still chorusing to the young-eyed cherubim. Such harmony is in immortal souls, but while this muddy garment of decay grossly encloses it in, we cannot hear it.
[Enter Musicians.]
Come, ho! And wake Diana with a hymn. With sweetest touches pierce your mistress's ear, and draw her home with music.
[Music.]
JESSICA. I am never merry when I hear sweet music.

LORENZO. The reason is, your spirits are attentive. Just observe a wild and wanton herd, or a race of youthful unbroken colts, making mad bounds, bellowing and neighing loud, which is the hot condition of their blood—if they happen to hear a trumpet sound, or any strain of music touch their ears, you'll see them all come to a mutual stop, their savage eyes turned to a modest gaze by the sweet power of music. That's why the poet pretended that Orpheus drew trees, stones, and floods, since nothing is so stocklike, hard, and full of rage but music for a while changes its nature. The man who has no music in himself, nor is moved by the concord of sweet sounds, is fit for treasons, stratagems, and spoils. The motions of his spirit are dull as night, and his affections dark as Erebus. Let no such man be trusted. Listen to the music.
[Enter Portia and Nerissa.]
PORTIA. That light we see is burning in my hall. How far that little candle throws his beams! So shines a good deed in a wicked world.
NERISSA. When the moon shone we didn't see the candle.

PORTIA. So does the greater glory dim the lesser. A substitute shines as brightly as a king until a king is by, and then his state empties itself, as does an inland brook into the main of waters. Music! Listen!
NERISSA. It's your music, madam, from the house.
PORTIA. Nothing is good, I see, without context. It sounds much sweeter than by day, I think.
NERISSA. Silence bestows that virtue on it, madam.

PORTIA. The crow sings as sweetly as the lark when neither is being attended to. And I think the nightingale, if she sang by day when every goose is cackling, would be thought no better a musician than the wren. How many things by their season are seasoned to their right praise and true perfection! Peace! How the moon sleeps with Endymion, and would not be awakened!
[Music ceases.]
LORENZO. That is the voice of Portia, or I am much deceived.
PORTIA. He knows me as the blind man knows the cuckoo—by the bad voice.
LORENZO. Dear lady, welcome home.
PORTIA. We have been praying for our husbands' welfare, which speed, we hope, the better for our words. Are they returned?
LORENZO. Madam, they are not yet. But a messenger has come ahead to announce their coming.
PORTIA. Go in, Nerissa. Give orders to my servants to take no notice of our being absent from here. Nor you, Lorenzo. Jessica, nor you.
[A tucket sounds.]
LORENZO. Your husband is at hand. I hear his trumpet. We're no tell-tales, madam, don't worry.
PORTIA. This night seems like only daylight ill—it looks a little paler. It is a day such as the day is when the sun is hid.
[Enter Bassanio, Antonio, Gratiano and their Followers.]
BASSANIO. We should hold day with the Antipodes, if you would walk in absence of the sun.
PORTIA. Let me give light, but let me not be light—because a light wife makes a heavy husband, and never may Bassanio be so for me. But God sort all out! You are welcome home, my lord.
BASSANIO. Thank you, madam. Give welcome to my friend. This is the man, this is Antonio, to whom I am so infinitely bound.
PORTIA. You should in every sense be much bound to him, because, as I hear, he was much bound for you.
ANTONIO. No more than I am well acquitted of.
PORTIA. Sir, you are very welcome to our house. It must show in other ways than words, so I'll keep this passing courtesy brief.
GRATIANO.
[To Nerissa.] By yonder moon I swear you do me wrong.
Honestly, I gave it to the judge's clerk. I wish he were gelded who has it, for my part, since you take it, love, so much to heart.
PORTIA. A quarrel, ho, already! What's the matter?
GRATIANO. About a hoop of gold, a paltry ring she gave me, whose inscription was for all the world like a cutler's poetry on a knife: "Love me, and leave me not."

NERISSA. What do you mean talking about the inscription, or the value? You swore to me when I gave it to you, that you would wear it till your hour of death, and that it should lie with you in your grave. Even if not for me, then for your vehement oaths, you should have been respectful and kept it. Gave it to a judge's clerk! No, God be my judge, the clerk who got it will never grow hair on his face.
GRATIANO. He will, if he lives to be a man.
NERISSA. Yes, if a woman lives to be a man.

GRATIANO. Now, by this hand, I gave it to a youth, a kind of boy, a little undersized boy, no taller than yourself, the judge's clerk—a prating boy who begged it as a fee. I couldn't for my heart deny it to him.

PORTIA. You were to blame—I must be plain with you—to part so casually with your wife's first gift, a thing put on with oaths upon your finger, and so riveted with faith unto your flesh. I gave my love a ring, and made him swear never to part with it, and here he stands. I dare swear for him he wouldn't leave it nor pluck it from his finger for all the wealth the world possesses. Now, honestly, Gratiano, you give your wife too unkind a cause of grief. If it were me, I should be mad about it.
BASSANIO.
[Aside.] Why, I'd better cut my left hand off,
and swear I lost the ring defending it.

GRATIANO. My Lord Bassanio gave his ring away to the judge that begged it, and indeed deserved it too. And then the boy, his clerk, who took some pains in writing, he begged mine—and neither man nor master would take anything but the two rings.
PORTIA. What ring did you give, my lord? Not that, I hope, which you received from me.
BASSANIO. If I could add a lie unto a fault, I would deny it. But you see my finger doesn't have the ring on it—it is gone.
PORTIA. Just as void is your false heart of truth. By heaven, I will never come into your bed until I see the ring.
NERISSA. Nor I in yours till I again see mine!

BASSANIO. Sweet Portia, if you knew to whom I gave the ring, if you knew for whom I gave the ring, and could imagine for what I gave the ring, and how unwillingly I parted with the ring, when nothing would be accepted but the ring, you would abate the strength of your displeasure.

PORTIA. If you had known the virtue of the ring, or half the worthiness of her that gave the ring, or your own honor to keep the ring, you would not then have parted with the ring. What man is there so much unreasonable, if you had wished to defend it with any terms of zeal, would have lacked the modesty to urge the thing held as a ceremony? Nerissa teaches me what to believe: I'll die for it but some woman had the ring.

BASSANIO. No, by my honor, madam, by my soul, no woman had it, but a civil doctor, who refused three thousand ducats from me, and begged the ring, which I denied him, and let him go displeased away—even he that had upheld the very life of my dear friend. What should I say, sweet lady? I was forced to send it after him. I was beset with shame and courtesy. My honor would not let ingratitude besmear it so much. Pardon me, good lady. By these blessed candles of the night, had you been there, I think you would have begged the ring of me to give to the worthy doctor.

PORTIA. Let that doctor never come near my house. Since he has got the jewel that I loved, and that which you swore to keep for me, I'll become as generous as you. I won't deny him anything I have—no, not my body, nor my husband's bed. I shall know him, I'm well sure of it. Don't sleep a night away from home. Watch me like Argus. If you don't, if I'm left alone, now by my honor (which is still my own), I'll have that doctor for my bedfellow.
NERISSA. And I his clerk. Therefore be well advised how you leave me to my own protection.
GRATIANO. Well, do so. Let me not catch him then, because if I do, I'll mar the young clerk's pen.
ANTONIO. I am the unhappy subject of these quarrels.
PORTIA. Sir, don't grieve. You are welcome notwithstanding.
BASSANIO. Portia, forgive me this enforced wrong, and in the hearing of these many friends I swear to you, even by your own fair eyes, in which I see myself—
PORTIA. Mark that! In both my eyes he doubly sees himself, in each eye one. Swear by your double self—and there's an oath of credit.
BASSANIO. No, but hear me. Pardon this fault, and by my soul I swear I will never more break an oath with you.

ANTONIO. I once did lend my body for his wealth, which but for him that had your husband's ring would have quite miscarried. I dare be bound again, my soul upon the forfeit, that your lord will never more break faith advisedly.
PORTIA. Then you shall be his surety. Give him this, and tell him to keep it better than the other.
ANTONIO. Here, Lord Bassanio, swear to keep this ring.
BASSANIO. By heaven, it is the same I gave the doctor!
PORTIA. I had it from him. Pardon me, Bassanio—because by this ring, the doctor lay with me.
NERISSA. And pardon me, my gentle Gratiano, because that same undersized boy, the doctor's clerk, in exchange for this, lay with me last night.
GRATIANO. Why, this is like the mending of highways in summer, where the ways are fair enough. What, are we cuckolds before we've deserved it?

PORTIA. Don't speak so grossly. You are all amazed. Here is a letter; read it at your leisure. It comes from Padua from Bellario. There you'll find that Portia was the doctor, Nerissa there, her clerk. Lorenzo here will witness that I set out as soon as you did, and only just returned. I haven't yet entered my house. Antonio, you are welcome, and I have better news in store for you than you expect. Unseal this letter soon. There you'll find that three of your merchant ships have richly come to harbor suddenly. You shall not know by what strange accident I chanced upon this letter.
ANTONIO. I am speechless.
BASSANIO. Were you the doctor, and I didn't know you?
GRATIANO. Were you the clerk that is to make me a cuckold?
NERISSA. Yes, but the clerk that never means to do it—unless he lives until he be a man.
BASSANIO. Sweet doctor, you shall be my bedfellow. When I am absent, then lie with my wife.
ANTONIO. Sweet lady, you have given me life and living. Because here I read for certain that my ships are safely come to harbor.
PORTIA. How now, Lorenzo! My clerk has some good comforts for you too.
NERISSA. Yes, and I'll give them to him without a fee. There I give to you and Jessica, from the rich Jew, a special deed of gift, after his death, of all he dies possessing.
LORENZO. Fair ladies, you drop manna in the way of starved people.
PORTIA. It is almost morning, and yet I'm sure you're not satisfied with these events in full. Let's go in, and there ply us with interrogatories, and we'll answer everything faithfully.

GRATIANO. Let it be so. The first interrogatory my Nerissa shall be sworn on is whether till the next night she'd rather wait, or go to bed now, with two hours to dawn. But were the day come, I should wish it dark till I were lying with the doctor's clerk. Well, while I live, I'll fear no other thing so sore as keeping safe Nerissa's ring.
[Exit.]
